text: The node builds the model's context itself, from the `/issues` bundle the page already has: the lead and its sentence, the digest, every watched issue's state and values, the open alerts, and the documentation for the part in focus. On a node whose alert engine is `shadow` or `events`, the open alerts leave out those of the heat and air packs the events replaced, since nobody can answer them there. The browser sends only the end of the thread: the question and the three exchanges before it. The Wall's narration (`prompt: wall`) is offered no tools, so the model answers without thinking, and has a context of its own, short facts anybody walking past may read: what is usual for the place, and none of the house's learnings, digests, things, alerts' words or who answered ([API](api.md#post-ask)). That context, and every tool result the model reads, has no coordinate, no sensor or station name, no sensor id and no `meta`. The node removes or replaces them before the model sees anything. Nothing is stored. The thread lives in the browser tab. It survives a reload, and goes when the tab closes, when somebody presses **new conversation** in the pane's header, or after half an hour with no question. The node writes no transcript, no database row and no log line with a word in it; the log says which tool ran and for how long. `GET /ask/status` answers `stored: false`.

title: Ask the node · Which model answers
text: Set up → Model decides, with the online key under Keys, for the pane and the Telegram bot alike. `planetai config` sets the same keys. | setting | what it does | |---|---| | `AGENT_REMOTE_URL`, `AGENT_REMOTE_MODEL` | a bigger model on another machine of yours. Ollama on a laptop is `http://<laptop>.local:11434/v1`, with `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` set on the laptop so it listens beyond itself | | `AGENT_ONLINE_URL`, `AGENT_ONLINE_MODEL`, `AGENT_ONLINE_KEY` | an online model: Anthropic, OpenAI or any other that speaks the OpenAI chat API | | `AGENT_PREFER` | `private` (the default): the model on your network, then this machine's, and never online, which includes a remote model at a public address. `fallback`: your network, then online, then this machine. `strongest`: online first | The pane tries them in that order and skips a model that does not answer for five minutes. It reaches the model on this machine only when `planetai agent local` set one up, so a node with no local model can still answer from a laptop on its network. [The bot](bot.md#the-ladder) has the ladder in full. With `fallback` or `strongest` you give up control of what is asked: the question and the page's context go to the provider named in `AGENT_ONLINE_URL`. That is their sentences and numbers, never a coordinate, a sensor's name or its id, because the pane removes those before any model reads them. The header says so in bold whenever an online model is in the order, every answer that came from it says `runs online at <host>`, and the fine print says the provider keeps what its own terms say it keeps. The node still keeps nothing.

title: Ask the node · Three ways to give it a voice
text: With no model set up, the pane says so, offers the documentation search, and shows three cards with a copy button. - A model on this machine. The card names the tag `planetai agent local` suggests for this machine's memory, its size, and the line to run on the node: `planetai agent local pull <tag>`. `planetai agent local` sets up Ollama and the loop first, and neither downloads anything until you pull. - A model on another machine of yours: `AGENT_REMOTE_URL` and `AGENT_REMOTE_MODEL` under Set up → Model, as in the table above. It stays on your network; at an address outside it, it counts as online. - Your own agent, over MCP. The card prints the `claude mcp add` line with this node's address, and `planetai agent` on the node prints the token. A remote agent gets the whole MCP surface; see [Bring your own agent](agents.md). When the model is installed and not answering, the pane says so and names `planetai doctor`. The next part to add is a pack: [packs](packs.md).

title: The bot and the model ladder
text: The bot adds conversation to a node. Somebody in the house asks "is the air bad right now?" on Telegram and gets an answer read from the node's own tools. Somebody says "I closed the windows" and the bot records it, in their words, as an act. A node needs none of this. It reads its sensors, evaluates its rules, writes its report and sends its alerts with no model anywhere. The model is a client of the node: it runs in its own container, `agent`, running `app/agent_loop.py`, which `planetai agent local` starts. Alerts and reports never pass through it. The app container writes and sends them, including the alert events of `ALERT_ENGINE=events` ([Alerts](alerts.md)), and the agent container has no clock and sends nothing on a schedule.

title: The bot and the model ladder · Setting it up
text: 1. **Start the loop.** Run `planetai agent local`. It installs Ollama if it is missing (Homebrew on a Mac, Ollama's script on Linux), starts it as a service, adds the compose profile `agent`, and builds and starts the container. It downloads no model. With none on the machine it says "no model is on this machine yet, and this command does not fetch one." and prints the recommendation for the machine's memory: `qwen3.5:4b` (3.4 GB on disk), or `qwen3.5:9b` (6.6 GB) at 16 GB and up. On Linux it sets `OLLAMA_URL=http://172.17.0.1:11434` and warns that Ollama must listen on `0.0.0.0` for the container to reach it. It ends by suggesting three things to send the bot. 2. **Pull a model when you want one.** `planetai agent local pull qwen3.5:4b` fetches it, sets `AGENT_MODEL` to that tag and recreates the agent container. It says "qwen3.5:4b is on this machine and AGENT_MODEL now points at it". With no tag it prints the right `pull` line for this machine. Until a model is pulled the loop answers from the remote or online rung if one is configured, and says so if none is. 3. **Ask it something.** Message the bot "is the node healthy?". It should answer in a sentence or two, after calling `health_check` and `status`. `planetai logs agent` shows whether Telegram is set, which ladder it built and how many tools it was given. The model must do tool calling. `docs/MODELS.md` lists five tags with their sizes and licences (`qwen3.5:4b`, `qwen3.5:9b`, `qwen3:4b`, `qwen3:8b`, `qwen3:1.7b`), and names `gemma3:4b` as a good small model that does not call tools. A container with no `AGENT_MODEL` set asks for `qwen3:4b`. `planetai agent stop` stops the container. Containers on macOS get the CPU only, on Intel and Apple Silicon alike, and the model is the one place on the node where that matters.

title: The bot and the model ladder · What the model is given
text: The loop hands the model 17 of the node's 21 MCP tools, the `read` ones and `act`. It cannot change a setting, run a pack's code, or make the node message the household by itself. Each time it opens a session the log says "tools withheld from the local model (admin): maintenance, report_now, run_pack_script, settings_set". Every rung gets the same 17, local, remote or online. A person driving an agent over the tailnet still has all 21 ([MCP](mcp.md)). `act` needs the person's own words. The tool refuses `acted`, `done`, `ok` or another placeholder as the note and tells the model to ask. > **Gap in v0.90.0.** The bot's system prompt tells the model to "give the exact command from `maintenance`" for a > task that needs the node's shell, and `maintenance` is one of the four tools the loop withholds. Asked to update or > back up the node, the bot cannot look the command up. The commands are in [The command line](cli.md).

title: The bot and the model ladder · The ladder
text: Three rungs, all speaking the OpenAI-compatible chat protocol with tools: | rung | what | settings | default model | |---|---|---|---| | `online` | Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini with a key; the only rung that sends anything off your network | `AGENT_ONLINE_URL` and `AGENT_ONLINE_KEY`, both required; an Anthropic URL also gets `x-api-key` | `AGENT_ONLINE_MODEL` = `claude-sonnet-4-6` | | `remote` | a bigger model on the tailnet: a laptop's Ollama, exo, llama.cpp. At a public address it counts as online | `AGENT_REMOTE_URL`, optional `AGENT_REMOTE_KEY` | `AGENT_REMOTE_MODEL` = `gpt-oss-120b` | | `local` | Ollama on this machine, always present | `OLLAMA_URL` + `/v1`; the container's `MODEL`, set from `AGENT_MODEL` | `qwen3:4b` | `AGENT_PREFER` sets the order. Its default, `private`, removes the online rung, so a node that never chose sends nothing off the network. `fallback` tries remote, then online, then local: online sits above local because a rung is skipped only when it fails, and a 4B model never fails, it answers weakly. `strongest` tries online, remote, local. A rung that raises an error is skipped for five minutes. The loop rebuilds the ladder from the node's settings every 60 seconds, so a change in Set up → Model takes effect without a restart. A value in `AGENT_ONLINE_URL` that is not a URL is logged and ignored. The dashboard's ask pane walks the same ladder from the same settings, so one choice governs both; see [Ask the node](ask.md). > **Gap in v0.90.0.** The Model group's description in Set up, on the classic dashboard and on the doors, still reads > "The strongest one the node can reach is used." The default is `private`, and `/model` in Telegram prints the order > in force. `tools/remote-model.sh gptoss` runs llama.cpp's server on a laptop or workstation with gpt-oss-120b (about 63 GB), or `qwen122b` for Qwen3.5-122B (about 75 GB), with an API key and tool calling on, and prints the `AGENT_REMOTE_*` lines for the node's `.env`. When the laptop is away the node falls back to its local model.

title: The bot and the model ladder · How it answers
text: Each question opens its own MCP session to `http://app:8080/mcp` with the admin token. The system prompt tells the model to use the tools and never guess a number: `health_check` and `status` for "how is it", `context` for the sea, the weather and the land, `readings` for history. It answers in the language `ALERT_LOCALE` names (English, Bahasa Indonesia or Spanish), opens with a fitting emoji, avoids statistics, records with `act` when a person says they did something, never reveals a token, and keeps to plain text under a hundred words without narrating. It gets up to eight rounds of tool calls at temperature 0.2, with the last six messages of the chat (three exchanges) as context. On the small local rung the model is told not to think aloud and its final answer is asked for as constrained JSON, because a 4B model otherwise narrates its reasoning. `<think>` blocks and Markdown are stripped before sending, since Telegram shows them raw. A message from a chat not in `TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS` is logged and not answered. The first one from each such chat since the loop started gets "This node answers its household only. To be added, ask whoever set it up to add this chat: <its id>." When no rung answers, the reply is "I can't answer questions right now. Alerts and the morning report still work. Whoever set up the node can fix this in Set up › Model.", and the log has the error. The bot's own fixed replies (the `/act` prompts, the errors, the picture and offer replies) are in English and Spanish, and fall back to English on a node set to Bahasa Indonesia. The model's answers follow `ALERT_LOCALE`.

title: The bot and the model ladder · Commands that need no model
text: These are templates over the node's tools and answer even when no model is reachable. | in Telegram | does | |---|---| | `/act 12 closed the windows` | records the action on alert 12 in those words, with the actor `<AGENT_NAME>/telegram`, and replies "Recorded what you did." | | `/act 12` | records nothing and asks "What did you do about it?", with the form to send it in: `/act 12 <what you did>` | | `/stack [issue]` | the issue's state, its sentence in your language, the four distances with their provenance and unit, and up to two open alerts (on a node whose alert engine is `shadow` or `events`, not the heat and air alerts an event stands for), read from the `issues` tool | | `/learned` | what the node learned here, from the `learned` tool: per learning, the alert as the household calls it and the verdict first ("An air alert: acting on it seemed to make it worse than leaving it (the finding holds)"), then its own sentence with the numbers. Empty until the first daily check, and it says why when `AGENT_PREFER` is not `private` | | `/learned day` · `week` · `month` · `year` | the newest diary entry of that size, as the morning message carries it | | `/learned smoke` | the five diary entries and learnings that best match the words, newest first among equals | | `/model [local\|remote\|online\|auto]` | pins a rung for this chat and prints the ladder: each rung, its model, its host, whether it is skipped right now, and what `AGENT_PREFER` means (`private`: "the node's own machines only, nothing leaves the network") | When the loop starts with Telegram set, it sets `TELEGRAM_BUTTONS=1`, and from then on the node's event messages carry three buttons: Done (`acted`), Not now (`acknowledged`) and Doesn't fit (`dismissed`). Pressing one posts `POST /actions` with `event_id`, `stage`, `actor` and `note`. Doesn't fit asks "What did you do instead?" and keeps the reply as the note. The button labels are in English, Indonesian and Spanish. `/act` answers an alert, never an event.

title: The bot and the model ladder · Sending a picture
text: A picture sent to the bot is kept on the node, the same as **+ Add an image** on the dashboard. The bot fetches it from Telegram and posts it to `POST /captures` ([API](api.md)) with the sender's first name as `actor`, the caption as the note, and `describe=1`. It answers "Kept." and says where the picture is and whether the image model (`EYES_MODEL`) is describing it. A picture the node already has (the same file, by its sha256) gets "That picture is already kept.", and one the node refuses gets the node's own reason. Pictures are the `eyes` pack's: with it off the node refuses every one, and the reply is "The node did not keep it: the eyes pack is off on this node". - Sent as a photo, Telegram recompresses it and drops its EXIF, so the node takes the largest size, dates it by the message and places it in the node's own cell. - Sent as a file (Telegram's *File* instead of *Photo*), the original reaches the node byte for byte. Its own date and GPS are used, then removed from the stored copy as with every capture. Send a picture taken somewhere else this way. - A tag in the caption names what took it: `#drone`, `#microscope`, `#camera` or `#balloon`, and none means `phone`. The tag is taken out of the note; any other `#word` stays in it. - A file that is not an image is refused, and so is one over 20 MB, the most the Bot API lets a bot fetch (send it as a photo, or add it from the dashboard). If the node refuses the bot's token, the reply asks whoever set up the node to check the bot's access, and the log has the status: the agent's `ADMIN_TOKEN` is not the app's. Only the household's chats (`TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS`) can send pictures; a picture from any other chat is logged and gets no reply. The download URL holds the bot token, so a failed download is logged by its error's type only. Telegram's location messages are not read, and the image model's description is on the image's card, not sent back.

title: The bot and the model ladder · Offers: someone who is not the household
text: A chat outside `TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS` gets no answer beyond the one line saying who the node answers, with one exception: an offer. An offer's `ask` link (`t.me/<bot>?start=offer-<id>`, in `GET /offers` and the daily export) opens the bot on that offer, and the bot asks for one message about the thing ("Write one message about the cordless drill (to borrow)…"). The next message, within 30 minutes, goes to every household chat with the offer's number and name, the message, and the sender's first name and @username. The sender is told "Passed on". You write back to them yourself through their @username. When they have none, both sides are told they can be reached only if the message said how. One message per chat an hour is passed on, and a later one is not. The household's chat ids never show, and nothing the sender writes is kept.

title: The bot and the model ladder · What leaves the network
text: Nothing, unless you give the online rung a key and set `AGENT_PREFER` to something other than `private`. The settings describe `AGENT_ONLINE_KEY` as "The only thing that lets household data leave your network." With `AGENT_PREFER=private` a key that is set is never used. The remote rung is meant for a machine of yours; the node reads its address, and a remote model at a public address (a city's server, a rented GPU) counts as online. With `AGENT_PREFER=private` it is not used at all. With `fallback` or `strongest` the bot hands it no settings, report bundle or day's export, the pane names it online, and agents stop reading what the house learned. The bot's writes appear in the audit trail as `<AGENT_NAME>/<rung>` (`local-model/local` by default), and tool arguments whose names contain `KEY`, `TOKEN` or `PASS` are masked in its log. > **Note.** Nothing checks the model's numbers. The report is written by the node from SQL; the bot's answers are the > model's, told to use the tools and not to guess.

title: The bot and the model ladder · Where this leads
text: The bot records an act the way every other surface does, as a row in `actions` that ρ counts: [ρ](rho.md). To put a stronger agent on the node, driven by a person, see [Bring your own agent](agents.md).

title: Channels
text: A channel is how an alert leaves the node and reaches the people it is for. This page connects four of them. Two (Telegram and Reticulum) also carry the answer back, which is how an alert becomes a row in `actions` and, from there, part of [ρ](rho.md). | channel | receives | needs internet | answers back | set up with | |---|---|---|---|---| | Telegram | every alert that reaches the floor; every report, the day's first with the morning memory; the bot's replies | yes | `/act <id> <words>`, and the event buttons, when the bot runs | `planetai telegram` | | Meshtastic (LoRa mesh) | `act` alerts, first line only | no | no | `planetai meshtastic`, then `MESH_ALERTS=1` | | Reticulum (LXMF) | `act` alerts, full text | no | `act <id> [note]` | `planetai reticulum` | | Home Assistant | every alert, sent or not, and every report sent, as entity state | no (LAN) | no | `planetai homeassistant` | Telegram, the mesh and Reticulum are all reached from `notify()` in `app/channels.py`. Home Assistant is a pack, `packs/home-assistant`, which hears every alert the node records through its `on_alert` hook, including the ones `notify()` does not send. With `ALERT_ENGINE=events` the heat and air-quality rules still record their alerts, and Home Assistant still gets them, but they are not sent. The event engine sends one message per event through the same `notify()`, so an `act` event reaches the mesh and Reticulum as well as Telegram. When and how often it sends is on [Alerts](alerts.md#the-event-engine).

title: Channels · Telegram
text: The default channel, and the one the report uses. Everything it sends is plain text prefixed with the level's icon (ℹ️ for info, ⚠️ for warn, 🔴 for act) unless the text opens with its own sign, as the report and most alerts do. Only Telegram carries an act alert's line on who in the house it matters to, and the morning memory. 1. **Run `planetai telegram`.** It prints `1. In Telegram, message @BotFather and send: /newbot`. Do that, give the bot any name and a username ending in `bot`, and copy the token BotFather replies with. 2. **Paste the token.** The node checks it with Telegram and prints `● token works. Your bot is @<name>`. A wrong token stops here with "Telegram rejected that token. Copy it again from @BotFather." 3. **Send the bot any message** (or add it to a group and make it an admin). The terminal waits up to two minutes, then prints `● found your chat: <id>`. It writes `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` and `TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS` to `.env` and to the running node's settings, so the terminal and the dashboard agree about which bot this node talks to. `TELEGRAM_CHAT_IDS` is a comma list, so several people can receive. 4. **Read the hello.** The chat receives `<NODE_NAME> is connected. Alerts will arrive here.` (in Spanish when `ALERT_LOCALE=es`). The terminal ends with `● the node is restarting with Telegram on. Try: planetai test-alert`. 5. **Run `planetai test-alert`.** A 🔴 message arrives. The whole path works: a rule fired, the node wrote a message, and it reached a person. With the token blank the node logs alerts and sends nothing. The node never logs the Telegram URL, because the token is in it, so `api.telegram.org/bot` in `planetai logs` would be a leak. Answering on Telegram is the [bot](bot.md), which runs in the separate `agent` container. `/act 12 closed the windows` records an `acted` row with the actor `<AGENT_NAME>/telegram` (`local-model/telegram` by default) and replies "Recorded what you did." `/act 12` with no words records nothing, and the bot asks "What did you do about it? Send it with your words: /act 12 <what you did>". `/act` answers alerts; an event is answered with its Done, Not now and Doesn't fit buttons, which the bot draws once it has announced itself (`TELEGRAM_BUTTONS=1`). `/stack` answers from the node's own arithmetic, with no model.

title: Channels · Meshtastic, the LoRa mesh
text: For sensors and alerts where there is no WiFi. One gateway radio with WiFi uplinks the mesh to an MQTT broker on the node, field radios carry a sensor on a battery, and a shelf radio paired to a phone receives alerts when the internet is down. 1. **Run `planetai meshtastic`.** It creates a broker user, starts the broker as the compose profile `mqtt`, and prints *Now the gateway radio (the ESP32 one), in the Meshtastic app* with every value to type: the LoRa region for your preset (`EU_868` by default, `SG_923` for Bali, `US` for Boston), MQTT on at `<this machine's LAN IP>:1883` with the username `planetai` and a generated password, encryption off, JSON output on (without it the node cannot read the packets), root topic `msh`, and uplink and downlink on for your channel. Nothing arrives until the gateway radio carries these values. 2. **Set the gateway and wait.** The terminal prints `Waiting for the first packet from the mesh (up to 3 minutes)`, then `● packets arriving. Sensors seen so far:` and the mesh sensors it has. Each radio's telemetry is now readings under its own sensor, `msh-<its node id>`, with the name the radio gives itself. A radio's own temperature and pressure are its enclosure, not the street. 3. **Turn on alerts back to the mesh.** Set `MESH_ALERTS=1` and `MESH_GATEWAY_NODE_NUM=<the gateway's node number, decimal>` in `.env`, then `planetai restart`. Once the node has learned the mesh's root topic from an uplink, an `act` alert's first line goes out through the gateway, and `planetai logs` shows `mesh -> sent <n> bytes on <topic>`. If step 2 prints nothing, the terminal names the usual reasons: JSON output off on the gateway, the wrong address, a gateway on another WiFi, or a firewall on 1883. A LoRa frame is about 200 bytes, a few a minute, enough for telemetry and one-line alerts and never for data between nodes. The boards, the firmware and the channel key are on [Radios](radios.md).

title: Channels · Reticulum, LXMF
text: **Read the licence before you turn it on.** The bridge installs `rns` and `lxmf`, which are under the [Reticulum License](https://github.com/markqvist/Reticulum/blob/1.5.4/LICENSE): MIT with two conditions, and not an open-source licence. You may not use them in a system that can purposefully harm people, or directly or indirectly in making a dataset to train an AI or machine-learning model. The node does neither. If you share the image you built, include that licence with it. What it means for the node is in [the decision record](https://github.com/fabcity/planetai-node/blob/main/docs/decisions/2026-10-23-reticulum-licence.md). The bridge has its own repository, [`fabcity/planetai-reticulum`](https://github.com/fabcity/planetai-reticulum), under Apache-2.0, so the node's own code never takes in `rns` or `lxmf`. It runs in its own container (compose profile `reticulum`) and gives the node an LXMF address that Sideband can message. It posts answers to `POST /actions` with `ACT_TOKEN`, and reads that token when its container is created, so run `planetai ui` first if the node has no `ACT_TOKEN` yet: it creates one. 1. **Run `planetai reticulum`.** It downloads the bridge at the commit this release pins, builds it on this machine, starts it and prints `● this node's LXMF address: <address>`, then what to do in Sideband: add a TCP Client interface to this machine's LAN address on port 4242, and start a conversation with the address above. A phone can now reach the node over Reticulum with no internet in between. 2. **Answer an alert.** Send `act 3 opened the windows`. The bridge records an `acted` row on alert #3 with the actor `lxmf:<your hash>` and replies `recorded: you acted on #3`. Sent as `act 3` alone, the note is recorded as `acted (via reticulum)`, because this path does not ask for words. 3. **Receive alerts.** Copy your own LXMF address from Sideband's settings into `.env` as `RETICULUM_ALERT_DESTINATIONS=<hash>[,<hash>]`, then run `planetai reticulum` again: the bridge reads the list when its container is created, and `planetai restart` recreates only the app. `planetai logs reticulum` then shows `bridge up: http :4243, announcing every 1800s, 1 alert destination(s), …` with your count. Every `act` alert is delivered, full text, to each address. To check, run `planetai test-alert`: Sideband shows a message from the node's address titled `planetai <NODE_NAME>`, with the whole test alert. If nothing arrives, `planetai logs reticulum` says `no path to <hash> yet; is that client announced and reachable?`. The bridge does not read `.env`. It receives eight variables from `docker-compose.yml`: `LOG_LEVEL`, `NODE_NAME`, `NODE_API_URL`, `RETICULUM_CONFIGDIR`, `RETICULUM_DATA`, `RETICULUM_ALERT_DESTINATIONS`, `RETICULUM_ANNOUNCE_S` and `ACT_TOKEN`. The Telegram token, the admin token and the database password stay out of a process whose job is to speak to a radio mesh. The transport is TCP; an RNode LoRa interface is a commented block in `config/reticulum/config`, copied from the bridge's `config.tpl` the first time. Presence is separate and off by default: with `RETICULUM_PRESENCE=1` the bridge announces the node's name and a coarse H3 cell every half hour, at `RETICULUM_PRESENCE_RES` (3) and never finer than resolution 6, whatever the setting says, so an exact place never leaves. `GET /presence` is what the bridge reads to do it, and it answers at every sharing level for that reason. Node-to-node data over Reticulum (a district and a community node with no internet between them) is not built; [`SPEC.md`](spec.md) §6 says what would bring it in.

title: Channels · Home Assistant
text: 1. **Run `planetai homeassistant`.** With no broker yet it says `● no broker yet: setting one up (this is the same broker the Meshtastic gateway uses)`. It sets `HA_DISCOVERY=1`, restarts the node, and prints `● publishing. Entities appear in HA within one poll (5 min).` with the broker address, port 1883, username and password. 2. **Add them in Home Assistant**: Settings → Devices & services → Add integration → MQTT. Discovery does the rest: a device per sensor, and a *latest alert* text sensor on the node itself. It is the `home-assistant` pack, switched on by `HA_DISCOVERY=1`. Each metric of each local sensor, and of the model and portal points, is published as a discovery entity, grouped under a device per sensor with a suggested area of Indoor or Outdoor. Other people's reference stations are not published. States are retained at `planetai/<node>/<sensor>/<metric>` and expire after an hour of silence. The *latest alert* sensor carries the first line of the latest alert or report, with `level`, `alert_id` and `ts` as attributes: every alert the node records, whatever its level and whatever quiet hours say, and every report that is sent. If Home Assistant already runs a broker, point `MQTT_HOST`, `MQTT_USER` and `MQTT_PASS` at it instead. The node switches nothing on or off. Build the automations in Home Assistant: purifier on above 35 for ten minutes, a window reminder at the cleanest hour, a phone notification when the alert level is `act`.

title: Channels · Languages
text: With `ALERT_LOCALE=es` the Telegram hello, the bot's own replies, the test alert, every alert and every report are in Spanish. With `id` the alerts and the report are in Bahasa Indonesia, and the bot's few fixed lines and the Telegram hello stay in English. The terminal is in English.

title: Channels · What a house with no internet still gets
text: A shelf radio paired to a phone receives the first line of every `act` alert over LoRa. Sideband receives the whole alert over LXMF and can answer `act <id>`. Home Assistant on the LAN keeps every entity current, and the dashboard on a wall screen keeps drawing. The node keeps polling its LAN sensors, running its rules and writing its reports; only Telegram waits for the internet to come back.

title: Channels · Where this leads
text: The node can now ask and hear the answer. [ρ](rho.md) is what it makes of the answers: the share of its alerts that somebody answered, and whether the condition stopped afterwards. The [report](report.md) is the one message it sends on a schedule rather than when a reading crosses a line.

title: Command line
text: `planetai` is how the person who keeps a node looks after it from the machine it runs on: install it, check it is alive, record what somebody did about an alert, change a setting, update it and keep its data safe. The commands that read or change a running node do it over its [API](api.md) on `localhost:$APP_PORT`, with the tokens in `.env`, so what they print is what the node is doing now. A few work without one: `planetai preflight` runs before there is a node, and `planetai sources` reads the pinned registry when the node does not answer. It is one bash script, `bin/planetai`, linked into `~/.local/bin`. It needs only the Python the machine already has (Apple's 3.9 on a Mac, standard library only). `planetai` on its own prints the command list. A word the node does not know gets "there is no `planetai <word>` in this node", the node's version, and the advice to run `planetai update`, because new commands arrive with releases. > **Gap in v0.90.0.** The list `planetai` prints leaves out four commands that exist: `preflight`, `sources`, > `config unset` and `agent local pull`. The tables below are complete. Only three things ask for `sudo`: `mesh` (to install and join Tailscale), `agent local` on a machine with `systemctl` where Ollama is not already answering, and `setup` when the installer has to install or start Docker. The installer says what each `sudo` is for before it asks.

title: Command line · Set up and remove
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai preflight [--json]` | Checks whether this machine can run a node. Installs nothing. Exit `0` go, `1` something you can fix (each ✗ says how), `2` no container runtime can run on this OS version. | | `planetai setup` | Runs the preflight, asks four questions (name, place, what the node is for, a Smart Citizen kit or none) and installs, with the city's [preset](configuration.md#presets) for a place in Bali, Barcelona, Boston or Santiago. Where a node exists it offers update, reconfigure, nothing or remove, and after an unfinished install it offers to carry on. | | `planetai setup --answers node.json` | The same install with no terminal, from a JSON file: `{"name": "my-node", "place": "Palma de Mallorca", "kind": "home", "sensor": {}}`. `lat` and `lon` can replace `place`; `sensor` is `{}` or one of `{"sc": "19880"}`, `{"sc_user": "you"}`, `{"airgradient": "host"}`, `{"purpleair": "ip"}`. See [Install](install.md). | | `planetai geocode <place>` | What the setup wizard would find for a place name, without installing anything. | | `planetai version` (`-v`, `--version`) | The version, the node's name and city, and the key it takes updates from: `updates signed by fabcity <fingerprint>`. | | `planetai remove [--keep-data]` (`uninstall`) | Asks twice (yes, then the node's name), removes the containers, the database (kept with `--keep-data`), the folder with any backups in it, the crontab line and the command, then checks nothing is left. |

title: Command line · Check on it
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai status [--json]` | Version, uptime, last poll and error, sensors, the last three alerts and ρ. | | `planetai doctor [quiet\|--guide\|--json]` | Every check, each failure with its fix, then the node's data sources. | | `planetai logs [service]` | Follows a container's log: `app` by default, or `db`, `agent`, `reticulum`, `mosquitto`. | | `planetai start` · `stop` · `restart` | `docker compose up -d`; `down`, data kept; recreate the app container, which is how a change in `.env` takes effect. | The doctor checks that Docker runs, the containers are up, the database answers, the node answers on its port and can log in to the database, the coordinates are set, `.env` has no space after an `=`, the backup folder is mounted, the captures folder is writable, a nightly backup is scheduled and more than 1 GB is free. With the `mqtt` profile it checks the broker and that mesh packets arrive; with `reticulum`, the bridge. A few rows state a fact rather than pass or fail: | row | what it says | when it is not green | |---|---|---| | `release signature verified on last update` | the last `planetai update` checked who built the tarball | red when that update ran with `PLANETAI_UNSIGNED=1` or predates signed releases. A git checkout has no such row. | | `source registry: N entries · awesome-fabcity-data @ <sha> · synced <date>` | which snapshot of the [source registry](sources.md) this node carries | red when `data/sources/REGISTRY_VERSION` is missing, amber when the pin is over 180 days old. Amber does not fail the run. | | `PLANETAI <version> is out` | a newer release exists | amber, never red. Absent when `UPDATE_CHECK` is off. | | `make: …` | `off` with the licence reason, or how many fab labs lie within `MAKE_RADIUS_KM`, from which snapshot | never. Shown only when the `make` pack is installed and `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE=1`. | Under the checks, **Data sources** lists what every node needs for its basic job, from [`GET /health/sources`](api.md), most important first. Each row is ✓, ✗ with its fix, or a dash when it does not apply or has not had its first poll: ``` Data sources ✓ Your own sensors 4 min ago · inside only; one outside would tell the house from the street ✗ Alerts on your phone (Telegram) not set up → Connect Telegram, two minutes: planetai telegram ✓ Air stations nearby 12 min ago ✓ Weather (Open-Meteo) 12 min ago ✓ Nightly backup 9 h ago ✓ The map of this place fetched 19 Oct 2026 ``` A cross here never changes the doctor's exit code, because a node without a sensor yet is still being set up. The map's fix is `planetai run place basemap`. `quiet`, which install, update and `planetai setup` use, ends with **To finish setting up**: the crosses again, each with its fix or the Set up address (`http://localhost:8080/#setup/sources`). `--guide` also offers, in a terminal, to do the first one. `--json` prints `{"ok": …, "checks": [{"check", "ok", "warn", "fix"}], "sources": [...]}`.

title: Command line · Reading the node
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai report` (`report now`) | Writes a report now, sends it, and prints it. | | `planetai report last` | The last report, when it was written, over how many hours, and whether quiet hours held it. | | `planetai act <id> [note]` | Records that you acted on alert `<id>`, with your login name as the actor, and prints ρ. | | `planetai sensors [--json]` | Every sensor the node reads, yours or reference, indoor or outdoor. | | `planetai cells [--json]` | The Index cells the node can fill, with value, state and unit. | | `planetai snapshot [--out FILE]` | One JSON file of what the node answers, read with the admin token, for a design round or a bug report. | `planetai act` is the terminal's way of closing a loop, and the note is the only record of what was done. Write it: ```bash planetai act 42 "closed the kitchen window and ran the purifier" ``` > **Careful.** With no note, `planetai act` records the word `acted`. The MCP `act` tool and Telegram's `/act` > refuse that word and ask for the person's own; the command line does not. On a node with `DECISION_REQUIRED=1` > an act with no decision recorded first is refused, and the command only says the node did not record it and asks > whether the alert id is real. `planetai snapshot` reads `/health`, `/issues`, `/stats`, `/alerts?limit=200`, `/rho`, `/cells`, `/observations`, `/sensors`, `/trust`, `/report/latest`, `/nearby`, `/forecast`, `/actions?limit=2000`, `/aggregates?hours=24`, `/reach`, `/earth`, `/shape`, `/effect` and `/issues/days?days=7`. The means from `/aggregates` land under `readings_1h`, joined with each sensor's `indoor`, `local` and `kind`. Every `note` in the actions is removed, since it is the household's own words, and a route that does not answer is listed under `provenance.refused`. The file, `snapshot-<node>-<YYYY-MM-DDTHHMM>.json` by default, holds no raw readings and no token.

title: Command line · Change it
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai config` | A guided walk through the setting groups. Changes are staged; `s` saves them, `q` cancels, `b` goes back. Needs a terminal. | | `planetai config --section G` | Straight into one group: `basics`, `sources`, `alerts`, `model`, `packs`, `keys`, `sharing`, `system` or `bootstrap`. | | `planetai config list [--section G]` | Every setting, the value in force and where it came from. Red when `.env` holds something else and is being ignored. | | `planetai config get KEY` | One setting: its help, the value in force, its source, and whether it needs a restart. | | `planetai config set KEY VALUE` | A runtime or pack key goes to the database and is live within 20 seconds. A bootstrap key goes to `.env`, and the command offers the restart. | | `planetai config unset KEY` | Removes the database value, so the key goes back to `.env` or the built-in default. | | `planetai config edit` | Opens `.env` in `$EDITOR` (nano by default), then offers a restart. | | `planetai report every N` | Hours between reports (`REPORT_EVERY`): 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24. | | `planetai report at H` | The local hour the report rhythm counts from (`REPORT_ANCHOR`), 0 to 23. | | `planetai report level act\|warn\|info` | What interrupts you between reports (`ALERT_LEVEL`). | | `planetai ui` (`dashboard`) | The dashboard's addresses, the `#wall` one included, the sharing level and the admin, backup and act tokens. Creates `ADMIN_TOKEN` and `ACT_TOKEN` if missing. | | `planetai test-alert` | Fires one act-level alert through every channel and waits up to 90 seconds for it. It adds a rule that fires within a minute and removes it as soon as its alert appears, so one message arrives. | The settings themselves, and what each one does, are on [Configuration](configuration.md).

title: Command line · Update and back up
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai update` | Backs up, fetches the release, checks its checksum and signature, migrates, rebuilds and verifies. Refuses at once when no container runtime is running. See [Updating](updating.md). | | `planetai backup` | Dump, export, remote copy and IPFS now, the job cron runs nightly at 03:17. | | `planetai restore <dump.sql.gz>` | Asks for the node's name, takes a safety backup, replaces the database with the dump and re-applies `init.sql`. Settings saved from Set up are not in a dump, so the node goes back to `.env`. With no file, lists the newest dumps. | | `planetai storage` | Where the database, backups, pictures, remote copy and exports are, and their state. | | `planetai storage set backups <dir>` | Where new dumps go (`BACKUP_DIR`). The folder must be mounted and writable. Dumps already made stay in the old folder, so keep it until you have copied them. | | `planetai storage set captures <dir>` | Moves where new pictures go (`CAPTURES_DIR`), checked the same way, then restarts the app. A NAS share is fine. Pictures already taken stay where they are. | | `planetai storage set remote <remote:path>` | After each backup, copies the dumps and exports off the machine with rclone (`BACKUP_REMOTE`). | | `planetai storage set keep <days>` | Days of dumps kept (`BACKUP_KEEP`). | | `planetai storage set data` | Refuses, and explains why the database stays on an internal disk. | | `planetai ipfs` | Starts Kubo (profile `ipfs`) and turns on publishing of each day's export; CIDs land in `exports/<node>/CIDS.txt`. | | `planetai grafana` | Starts Grafana (profile `grafana`) on loopback, with a read-only database login and a starter dashboard: your own panels over the node's readings. [Grafana](grafana.md). | | `planetai grafana off` | Stops it, takes it out of `COMPOSE_PROFILES` and drops its database login. Your own dashboards stay in the `grafana` volume. | Where the data lives, and why never on a network mount: [Storage](storage.md).

title: Command line · Channels and the network
text: | command | what it does | sudo | |---|---|---| | `planetai telegram` | Checks the bot token, waits up to two minutes for your first message to learn the chat id, saves both, sends a hello and restarts the app. | no | | `planetai homeassistant` (`ha`) | Starts the broker if there is none, sets `HA_DISCOVERY=1`, and prints what to enter in Home Assistant's MQTT integration. On a node that lists its packs in `PACKS_ENABLED`, add `home-assistant` there too. | no | | `planetai mesh [up\|status\|down]` | Installs Tailscale and joins your tailnet under the node's name, then prints how to reach it. `TS_AUTHKEY` in the environment joins without a browser. Records `MESH_NAME`. | yes | | `planetai reticulum` | Downloads the LXMF bridge from fabcity/planetai-reticulum at the commit `RETICULUM_REF` pins, builds it, starts it (profile `reticulum`), and prints the node's address and how to reach it from Sideband. | no | | `planetai hello [--remove]` | Lists this node on every node's map. It shows the entry a stranger would see (name, the centre of its cell, the place, who runs it, an optional contact) and opens the pull request to `registry.json` with `gh`, or prints the entry and the edit link. Once merged, nodes see it within the hour. `--remove` takes the node off. | no | See [Channels](channels.md) and [Federation](federation.md).

title: Command line · Radios and DIY nodes
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai meshtastic` | Starts the MQTT broker (profile `mqtt`), writes its password, prints the gateway radio's settings for your region, and waits up to three minutes for the first packet. | | `planetai broker` | Starts the same broker and prints what to type into a Smart Citizen Kit's shell or a DIY node's setup portal so it publishes here. Waits up to three minutes for the first message. | | `planetai radio` | On its own, a guide: each step ticked or not, the radios on USB now, and the next command. | | `planetai radio init [--region R] [--slot N] [--preset P] [--force]` | Writes the fleet file `config/radio/fleet.yaml`: two channel keys, the region from `NODE_CITY` and, in Bali, a frequency slot pinned inside Indonesia's 920 to 923 MHz. A city with no known region is refused until you pass `--region`. `--force` makes new keys, so every radio must be provisioned again. | | `planetai radio render <role> "<name>" <SHORT>` | Prints the settings `provision` would apply. | | `planetai radio provision <role> "<name>" <SHORT> --port P [--wifi SSID:PSK] [--mqtt ADDR USER PASS] [--fixed LAT,LON]` | Applies a role (`sensor`, `relay`, `shelf`, `gateway-wifi`, `gateway-host`) one settings section at a time, reboots the radio and reads it back over a new connection; the exit is non-zero if anything differs. `--fixed` pins a radio with no GPS, south latitudes as written (`--fixed -8.8,115.1`). | | `planetai radio url [--json]` | How to put a phone on the mesh: the channel link, and a QR when `qrencode` is installed. | | `planetai radio gateway --port P [--broker HOST:PORT] [--install] [--once]` | Makes a radio on this machine's USB the node's gateway. `--install` keeps it running as a service. | | `planetai radio federate [--write]` | Prints, and with `--write` installs, the broker's bridges to the nodes in `RADIO_PEERS`. Only `fabcity/` topics cross. | | `planetai radio list [--port P]` | The fleet file and, with a port, what that radio sees. | | `planetai radio doctor [--port P]` | The usual reasons nothing arrives, checked one by one. | `planetai radio` talks to radios from the host, so it needs `python3 -m pip install --user meshtastic paho-mqtt` there; it prints the exact line for your Python when they are missing. See [Radios](radios.md).

title: Command line · Packs and sources
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai packs` | What is loaded (or on disk, when the node is down), core and wild apart, where each wild pack came from, and whether `packs install` has work to do. | | `planetai packs add <id>` | Fetches a wild pack from the list at fabcity/planetai-wild-packs, at the commit it was listed at, into `packs/<id>`, then runs `packs install`. | | `planetai packs add <owner>/<repo>[/<folder>][@<ref>]` | The same for any pack on GitHub, pinned to the commit the ref names. Refuses an id a core pack already has. | | `planetai packs install` | Adds every pack's missing `env:` keys to `.env` under a dated marker, records their `pip:` lists and rebuilds the image once. | | `planetai run` | Lists every pack script with its first line. | | `planetai run <pack> <script> [args]` | Runs it inside the app container, with `PACK_OUT=/app/out` and the pack keys saved from Set up in its environment. | | `planetai sources [--all] [--pillar P] [--scale S] [--cell 'Pillar\|Scale'] [--json]` | What the source registry lists for this place: entries relevant to `NODE_CITY` or `global`, or all of them with `--all`. Reads the node, or `data/sources/index.json` when the node is down. | Each line is a slug, status, licence, the pilots it matters to, and the code that reads it (`core:ckan`, `pack:coast`, or blank when nothing on this node does). The counts below the list cover the whole registry, or one cell with `--cell`. With the snapshot v0.90.0 carries (`awesome-fabcity-data` at `cd90289`, 283 entries, synced 2026-10-24): ``` across 19 cells: capable 12 / reviewed 17 / candidate 55 capable = live with an adapter. reviewed = live, backed by an adapter or a usable review. candidate = verified, unread. ``` `--cell 'Governance|City' --all` lists 32 entries, `capable 4 / reviewed 4 / candidate 0`. With `--all` a last line names what no count includes: `8 deprecated, 1 paywalled, 3 planned, 4 stale`. The same list is `GET /sources`; see [The source registry](sources.md) and [Packs](packs.md).

title: Command line · Agents
text: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `planetai agent` (`agents`, `mcp`) | The MCP endpoint on this machine and the tailnet, the twenty-one tools by class (read, act, admin), the header to send and a ready `mcp.json` block. See [MCP](mcp.md). | | `planetai agent local` | Installs and starts Ollama, and starts the `agent` container that answers on Telegram ([The bot](bot.md)) and serves the ask pane ([Ask the node](ask.md)). It downloads no model, it names one: `qwen3.5:9b` (6.6 GB) at 16 GB of memory or more, else `qwen3.5:4b` (3.4 GB). | | `planetai agent local pull <tag>` | `ollama pull <tag>`, sets `AGENT_MODEL` to it and restarts the `agent` container. Without a tag it prints the recommended one. | | `planetai agent stop` | Stops the `agent` container. | A person driving an agent gets all twenty-one tools. The model on this machine, the `local` rung, gets the read and act tools only. [docs/MODELS.md](../../docs/MODELS.md) lists the model tags. `planetai status --json`, `doctor --json`, `sensors --json`, `cells --json`, `sources --json` and `preflight --json` print JSON for scripts and agents, and `planetai setup --answers` installs without a terminal. The MCP tool `maintenance` hands back the commands for `update`, `backup`, `restore`, `restart`, `logs`, `doctor` (as `planetai doctor --json`), `storage`, `ui` and `telegram` as text to run on the host, because the container has no Docker and no git.

title: Command line · Not commands
text: There is no `planetai publish`, `share`, `rho`, `model`, `decide` or `decisions`. `status` and `act` print ρ. `/model` is a command for the Telegram bot. The Index's own writer publishes to the Index, never a node ([Federation](federation.md)). Sharing is a setting, `SHARE_LEVEL`. A decision is recorded from the dashboard's Decide form; the terminal has no form for it.

title: Command line · Where this leads
text: [Configuration](configuration.md) is where the household decides what the node reads, when it speaks and what it lets out. If no sensor of yours is answering yet, [Sensors](sensors.md) is the next part to add.

title: Concepts
text: The words the other pages use, each with what it means in the code. Several come in pairs that sound alike and are not (`local` and `custody`, domain and issue, `kind` and `scale`, decided and acted). Most of them answer one question: which numbers belong to this place, and which may be counted for it.

title: Concepts · The node and its place
text: **Node.** The program at one address: two containers, one database, one API. It has a name (`NODE_NAME`, lowercase with dashes), a position (`NODE_LAT`, `NODE_LON`), a time zone (`NODE_TZ`) and a city key (`NODE_CITY`). Node #1 is `bayu-ungasan` in Kuta Selatan; node #2 is in Menorca. ![Nested H3 cells around the node, resolution 6 to 12](img/cell-ladder.svg "The edges are H3 averages. The node's own resolution 8 cell is drawn heavy.") **Kind** (`NODE_KIND`): `home`, `business`, `community` or `district`, what the node is for. No code reads it for a default or a pack; `/presence` announces it. It is separate from the Index scale; the setup wizard sets `NODE_SCALE=city` when the kind is `district`. **Scale** (`NODE_SCALE`): `community`, `city` or `region`, one of the Full Stack Metrics Framework's scales. It is stamped on every push and names the core's own cell, `Governance|<Scale>`. It changes no code. **The H3 cell.** The node stands in a hexagon of the H3 grid at resolution 8, with an edge of about half a kilometre: 497 m for node #1's cell, measured from the cell itself. The page prints it in the mono as a fifteen-character id such as `8895a4c843fffff`, with its edge length beside it. Resolution 8 is coarser than the three-decimal rounding of the node's position, so publishing the cell does not put the position back. **The ladder.** The same place at eleven rungs, resolution 2 to 12, opening at 8, on the dashboard and on the wall. Each rung carries one cell's size and how many stations fall in it. The node publishes its own resolution 8 cell, in `/health`, the export and the node list, and announces nothing finer than resolution 6 over Reticulum. Rungs finer than about 110 m are finer than the node says where it is, because `/health` rounds its position to three decimals. The node computes the whole table and the page draws it. **Issue.** What a household calls a quality of its place: `air`, `heat`, `land`, `coast`, `water`, with noise and energy designed. Declared one file each, an `issue.yml` in the pack that watches it, ordered by `NODE_ISSUES`, the keeper's order, most important first. An issue is *sensed* when it has eyes on it and rules that can ask for something, *context* when it informs and never asks. See [Issues](issues.md). **Domain.** What a pack declares it is about. There are more domains than issues: weather feeds air and heat, but nobody asks how the weather is doing as a quality of their place. `place` is the ground, `governance` the loop and the Index. Trust in the instruments has no pack: its rules are the core's.

title: Concepts · Sources and sensors
text: **Adapter.** One function returning `(sensors, readings)`. In `app/sources.py` for the sources that ship with the core; in a pack's `adapter.py` for a code pack. The contract is on the [sensors](sensors.md) page. **Sensor.** A row in `sensors`: `sensor_id`, `source`, `name`, `lat`, `lon`, `indoor`, `local`, `kind`, `scale`, `cadence`, `meta`. The id is `<source>-<upstream id>` (`sc-19880`, `bad-pa-46949`), stable and never reassigned. **`local`.** Two facts at once: an adapter says whether a sensor is *yours*, and the node checks whether it is *here*, within `LOCAL_RADIUS_M` (500 m) of the node. A kit on your account 1.2 km away is yours and is not this node's measurement. A sensor with no coordinates that arrives over your own gateway stays local. **`indoor`.** Carried on every sensor and honoured by every rule. An indoor sensor measures a room and never enters an ambient average. **`kind`.** How the number was produced: `sensor`, `portal`, `model`, `map`, `child` or `peer`. Two more kinds carry no measurement: `facility`, a named place with a point (a fab lab from the `make` pack), and `survey`, what the household tells the node (the `things:<node>` sensor of the things it keeps). Only `sensor` rows enter `stats`. **`custody`.** A generated column: `kind = 'child' OR (local AND kind <> 'peer')`. The only thing a cell may count. Custody splits geography from responsibility: a peer's station can be closer than your own kit and still never be counted. **Peer.** Another node whose numbers you may show and must never act on. A `kind='peer'` row reaches no cell, no custody count, no aggregate, no alert, no report line. **Channel role.** What a metric *is* for a given source, declared in `channels.yml` and written to `channel_roles`: `ambient` (the air, water or land at a place, comparable between sensors there), `enclosure` (the inside of the instrument's own box: a BME680 sealed in a radio reports the box, not the street), `device_health` (battery, radio utilisation), `derived` (computed by the node), `index` (a vendor's own composite, never pooled), `private` (the house's own: used here, never sent). **Metric names.** Lowercase, no units in the name, for example `pm25 pm25_raw pm10 pm1 temp humidity pressure aqi gas_resistance noise light eco2 tvoc co2 tvoc_index nox_index`. Units are fixed: µg/m³, °C, %, kPa. `pm25` is the published value; if a correction was applied, the uncorrected figure sits beside it as `pm25_raw`. Raw is never overwritten. **The four distances.** Where a reading comes from, nearest first. The wire keys are `room` (local, indoor), `yard` (local, outdoor), `ring` (somebody else's device near here) and `region` (a model, a portal). The page prints them as house · street · ring · region; in Bahasa, rumah · jalan · sekitar · wilayah. In Spanish they are casa · calle · alrededores · región. The keys stay as they are on the wire. A child node is a fifth place that is not a column. A distance says whose instrument it is and has no scale: nothing maps a distance to an H3 resolution. **Registry.** A pinned snapshot of `awesome-fabcity-data`, 283 entries at `cd90289`, served at `/sources` and listed by `planetai sources`. Most entries are things this place could measure; some are places to go and designs to build. See [The source registry](sources.md).

title: Concepts · Rules, alerts, actions
text: **Rule.** SQL that returns rows, plus a message template with `{placeholders}` for the row's columns, a `level` and a `cooldown_minutes`. There is no rules engine or expression language; if Postgres cannot express the condition, the condition is wrong. Core rules live in `config/rules.yml` and know no metric; a pack's rules live in `packs/<id>/rules.yml`, namespaced `<pack>/<id>`. A rule's message ends with its recommendation; where that line begins with 👉, the alert's card in Decide shows it as "what this node suggests". **Level.** `act`: something needs doing. `warn`: something changed. `info`: everything else. `ALERT_LEVEL` is the floor for interrupting a person; below it an alert is still recorded, still on the dashboard, still in the next report. **Alert.** A row in `alerts` (`ts`, `rule_id`, `sensor_id`, `level`, `text`), whether or not it was sent. Three paragraphs: what is happening, what it means, what to do. An act-level alert that no one has answered is an *open alert*. **Cooldown.** Per rule and sensor, enforced in SQL against `alerts`: a rule does not fire again for the same sensor until its cooldown has passed. **Action.** A row in `actions`: `alert_id`, `stage`, `actor`, `note`. `SPEC.md` calls this table "the Index's instrument, not an app feature", and ρ is computed from it and nowhere else. A row has one of six stages: | stage | means | |---|---| | `acknowledged` | someone saw it | | `acted` | someone did the thing | | `decided` | someone said what will be done; it moves nothing | | `measured` | the outcome was checked; the schema allows it, nothing writes it, and the funnel derives it instead | | `settings` | an audit row for a setting change, with no alert | | `dismissed` | an alert event's advice did not fit the house | `POST /actions` takes `acknowledged`, `acted` or `decided` for an alert, and `acknowledged`, `acted` or `dismissed` for an alert event. **Alert event.** One story per issue per house, folded from the rows of rules that declare a `kind`: it opens, escalates and clears, and has at most one action chosen from what is inside, outside and in the home. It is a row in `alert_events`, its messages are in `event_messages`, and `GET /issues` carries it under `events`. It runs with `ALERT_ENGINE=shadow` (records what it would send, sends nothing) or `events` (sends); the default, `rules`, runs no engine. Its answers are Done (`acted`), Not now (`acknowledged`) and Doesn't fit (`dismissed`), posted with an `event_id`. Done and Not now on an event sent at act level count in ρ; Doesn't fit does not. On `shadow` and `events` the event stands for the alerts of the heat and air rules it replaced: those are no longer open alerts, and an issue's state follows its event. See [Alerts](alerts.md). **Decision.** A `decided` row, recorded from an alert's card in Decide. It closes no alert, is not in ρ and is not a stage in the funnel. With `DECISION_REQUIRED=1` (off by default) an `acted` with no `decided` row before it is refused with HTTP 409. **ρ (rho).** The share of act-level alerts in the last 30 days that had an `acknowledged` or `acted` action within 24 hours, pooled with the children's events. It is the one number on the page that comes from a person. See [ρ](rho.md). **Funnel.** The same alerts counted four times: asked, acknowledged, acted, measured. `measured` is derived: an act followed by 2,880 minutes (48 hours) of silence from the same rule on the same sensor, for rules the node still runs. The funnel counts this node's own alerts only. **Effect.** `GET /effect`, per rule over the whole record: how many acts, how many *cleared* (the same derivation), and a recovery time in hours only for a rule that declares `watch: {metric, over}`. **Contributor.** A rule with `contributes: report` and no message. It is never sent; its first row lands in the report bundle under the rule's id. **Report.** The node's one scheduled message: every `REPORT_EVERY` hours from `REPORT_ANCHOR`, local time, four parts, under a hundred words, written by the node itself from SQL. See [The report](report.md).

title: Concepts · The page and its stages
text: **Stages.** The loop runs observe, decide, act, measure, and the dashboard has a stage for each; Now draws Decide first. Every section the page draws is registered under one of them. **Digest.** Four sentences, one per stage, written by the node in English, Bahasa Indonesia and Spanish from figures already in `GET /issues`. Beside them, `digest.simple` is the paragraph simple mode draws, and `digest.prompts` the questions the ask pane offers, three at a time. **Headline.** The issue the lead is about. The issue of the most serious open alert event leads first. After that the highest state wins; between two issues in the same state, the one that moved most in the last three hours; an exact tie goes to the order in `NODE_ISSUES`. Only an issue that declares a `hero` (how it is drawn when it leads) can lead. The page prints that rule under the lead, and `lead: {issue, by}` says which of the four steps picked it: `event`, `state`, `moved` or `order`.

title: Concepts · Packs
text: **Pack.** A folder in `packs/` with a `pack.yaml`. A *core* pack ships in this repository; every other pack is *wild*, added with `planetai packs add` and pinned to a commit, and marked by a `.wild` file. A *data pack* is YAML only: rules, cells, channel roles. A *code pack* also ships Python (an `adapter.py`, `hooks.py`, `routes.py` or scripts); its adapter and hooks run only when `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE=1`, or, for a core pack that names its own `switch:`, when that switch is on. The `make` pack, which names the nearest fab lab, needs `MAKE_ENABLED=1` as well, because the directory it reads is not openly licensed. See [Packs](packs.md).

title: Concepts · The Index and its cells
text: **Cell.** One of the twenty cells of the Fab City Index, four pillars (Environmental, Economic, Social, Governance) by five scales (Community, City, Region, Bioregion, Planet), written `Pillar|Scale`. A node can fill cells at any scale with the same code; what changes is the kind of source. A pack's `cells.yml` computes a value with SQL that returns one `value`. The core adds `Governance|<Scale>`, which is ρ and reads `partial` until five act-level alerts have been answered within a day. `planetai cells` lists what a node fills. ![Twenty Index cells, four pillars by five scales](img/index-cells.svg "Community, City and Region roll up from nodes; Bioregion and Planet only send context downward.") What a cell needs at each scale: | scale | describes | arrives as | cadence | `kind` | |---|---|---|---|---| | Community | this address, this lab | a device you own, or a nearby public sensor | minutes | `sensor` | | City | a district, a municipality | an open-data portal, a municipal network | days | `portal` | | Region | a province, a metro | statistical APIs, grid operators | months | `portal` | | Bioregion | a watershed, a biome | hydrology, biodiversity, satellites | months to years | `portal`, `model` | | Planet | boundary conditions | Earth models sampled at your coordinates | hours | `model` | **State.** Where the number came from, which is a different question from how sure it is. `live` means measured here, in custody, in the last 24 hours; a model or a portal is `partial` whatever its quality, as is anything derived; `mock` means a placeholder. The core demotes `live` to `partial` when there are too few hourly buckets or too few sensors, and aggregation never upgrades it. A cell with no source stays empty: the node does not fill what it cannot measure. **Aggregation stops at Region.** Community, City and Region roll up from nodes. Bioregion and Planet enter as boundary conditions, context published downward and never rolled up, which is the Index's own methodology.

title: Concepts · Reaching the node
text: **`SHARE_LEVEL`.** What a request with no token may read. At `off` that is the dashboard shell, `/health`, `/presence`, `/llms.txt`, the daily export, the programme's node list at `/nodes`, `/offers` while the `things` pack is on, and `/settings` reduced to the layout and the sharing level. At `open` it is the whole read API, which is what a wall screen without a token needs, plus the map's public layers under `/ground/*` and `/geo/cell` without its node-relative fields. Two more levels, `cell` and `means`, are named and refused. Every untrusted JSON answer names the house's rooms and sensors only as "Room A" and "Sensor 1". See [Sharing](sharing.md). **Tokens.** `ADMIN_TOKEN` unlocks every write and the agent surface. `BACKUP_TOKEN` is read-only, for a NAS pulling dumps and the report bundle. `ACT_TOKEN` closes a loop, from a phone or from the dashboard's **I did this**, and can read no secret. `AGGREGATE_TOKEN` is what this node demands from its children; it opens only `POST /aggregates` and `POST /events`, and anything else a child asks is answered as to a stranger. `PARENT_TOKEN` is what it presents to its parent. All travel as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. **Loopback.** A request from `127.0.0.1` inside the container (the node's own MCP tools, a shell in the container) is trusted without a token. A browser on the host machine arrives from Docker's bridge and is not loopback. **Parent and child.** A child posts the hourly means of its own sensors to its parent's `/aggregates` and alert timestamps to `/events`; the parent stores the means under `<child>/<sensor_id>` with `kind='child'`. Raw never travels the link. See [Federation](federation.md). **The tailnet.** Tailscale, joined with `planetai mesh`. The node is reachable by its MagicDNS name, `<name>.<your-tailnet>.ts.net`, from your devices with no open port. This is how you reach it from outside; do not forward a port.

title: Concepts · Provenance words on the page
text: `live`: measured by this node, in the house or on the street. `partial`: derived, a portal, the ring. `model`: a model row. `cached`: a committed fixture replayed through the node's own engine. `stale`: the last figures the node gave, once it has stopped answering. When a poll fails the lead's pill says `stale` and the as-of stamp says "Read at HH:MM · the node has not answered for N min"; the classic wall's foot carries a fixed `stale` label, and the doors' Wall says it only when its last poll is over 15 minutes old. `refused` is a whole page: what a reader without a token sees at `SHARE_LEVEL=off`, with the node's own sentence explaining why. Provenance words are drawn in ink, in a square box, and never as a coloured pill.

title: Concepts · Words
text: The dashboard and these pages use the programme page's words for what a person reads. The wire keys and fields behind them stay as they are. | The word a person reads | What it means | Wire key or field behind it | Retired word | |---|---|---|---| | alert | what the node sends a person when an act-level rule crosses its line | `alerts`, `asks` in `GET /issues` | ask | | open alert | an act-level alert no one has answered yet | `open_asks` on each issue | open ask | | ladder | the control that sets the H3 resolution, 2 to 12 | `geometry.grain_table`, the `res` query key | rail, grain rail, dial | | rung | one step of the ladder: one H3 resolution | `res` on each `grain_table` row | stop, grain | | resolution | how fine a cell is, as an H3 number | `res` | grain | | house | local and indoors | `room` | room | | street | local and outdoors: the household's own kit outside | `yard` | wall outside | | ring | somebody else's public stations near here | `ring` | street | | region | a model or a portal for this point | `region` | model | The retired words stay out of every other page.

title: Concepts · Where this leads
text: These words are enough to read [How it works](how-it-works.md) end to end. To see them on a running node, [install](install.md) one.

title: Configuration
text: A setting is a decision the household makes about its node: which sensors count as its own, what it watches first, when it may interrupt somebody, what a stranger on the WiFi may read, whether a question may leave the house for an online model. This page lists every setting a node has, where its value comes from and what it defaults to, grouped by what the node does with it. At v0.90.0 that is 62 runtime keys, 20 bootstrap keys, 42 keys declared by packs, and the keys read only from the environment.

title: Configuration · How a setting is read
text: The base is `.env` in the node's folder. `install.sh` writes it, it holds the tokens and the database password, and it is never committed: keep it `chmod 600`. Docker hands the whole file to the `app` and `agent` containers and to nothing else. The `reticulum` container gets eight named variables only: `LOG_LEVEL`, `NODE_NAME`, `NODE_API_URL`, `RETICULUM_CONFIGDIR`, `RETICULUM_DATA`, `RETICULUM_ALERT_DESTINATIONS`, `RETICULUM_ANNOUNCE_S` and `ACT_TOKEN`. A **runtime** setting can be overridden in the database, from the dashboard's Set up view, `planetai config set`, `PUT /settings` with the admin token, or the MCP `settings_set` tool. The database value wins over `.env` and the node has it within about 20 seconds, with no restart. Saving a blank value deletes it, and the key falls back to `.env`, then to the built-in default. `GET /settings` gives each value's source as `gui`, `env` or `default`, and the `default` a fresh node gets, read from `data/env_defaults.yml` (generated from `.env.example`). A **bootstrap** setting is read once, when Docker composes the containers or the process starts. The dashboard shows these read-only; change one in `.env` and run `planetai restart`, or let `planetai config set` do both. An **env only** key is read from the environment and nowhere else. `GET /settings` does not list it and `planetai config set` says it is not a setting this node has: edit `.env` and restart. The terminal side of all this, `planetai config` and its shortcuts, is on [the command line](cli.md#change-it). ### Keys the packs declare A pack lists its keys under `env:` in its `pack.yaml`, with a comment above each. `GET /settings` shows the keys of every installed pack, switched on or not, in the group `packs`, so you can see a pack's switch before you turn it on. They are set like runtime keys, and `PUT /settings` answers 400 only for a key nothing declares. Because a pack reads its keys from the environment, the node puts the database value there too, and the pack has it at its next run. A key the pack also lists under `secrets:` is masked once saved, like the node's own tokens. `planetai packs install` appends the keys a `.env` is missing, under a dated marker. `COAST_MAX_KM`, `EE_PROJECT` and `EE_KEY_FILE` are pack keys and runtime keys at once. `GET /settings` lists each once, in `packs`, with the pack's name beside it. ### Public, outward, secret An anonymous `GET /settings` sees the value of a **public** key only; every other value shows as `•••• set` until the admin token is presented. At `SHARE_LEVEL=off`, a caller who is neither on this machine nor carrying a token sees only `UI_LAYOUT` and `SHARE_LEVEL`. A **secret** is masked for everyone, always; `GET /settings/raw` with the admin token is the one unmasked read, and it covers runtime keys only. An **outward** key changes what leaves the machine. Set up asks before saving a change to one, and before saving `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE=1` (`runs_code` in `GET /settings`), in a panel that quotes the setting's own help. Most settings are free text, so a typo does not stop the node. Thirteen keys accept only the values in their Values column below, and `PUT /settings` answers 400 for anything else: `REPORT_EVERY`, `REPORT_ANCHOR`, `REPORT_DEPTH`, `LEARN_PUSH`, `ALERT_ENGINE`, `UI_MODE`, `AGENT_PREFER`, `SHARE_LEVEL`, `UI_ASK`, `UI_GROUND`, `MAP_TILES`, `UPDATE_CHECK` and `SPECIES_MATCH`. `GET /settings` lists them under `choices`, so the dashboard and `planetai config` offer the values instead of a text box. ### Rules of the `.env` file - No space after `=`. `VAR= value` is a shell command, not an assignment. - A comment goes above a key that ships blank, never after it: `KEY= # note` hands the container `# note` as the value. - A number left blank keeps the code default. `update.sh` copies new keys into your `.env` with the value `.env.example` gives them, and the `REPORT_*` keys ship blank so an updating node keeps the rhythm it had. - `planetai doctor` checks for stray spaces, and `update.sh` refuses to run until they are gone. An older `.env` may still hold these, and nothing reads them: | key | what happened to it | |---|---| | `BRIEFINGS`, `BRIEF_MORNING`, `BRIEF_EVENING`, `BRIEF_HOUR` | Replaced by the report rhythm. A node that had `BRIEF_MORNING=7` was set once to `REPORT_EVERY=12`, `REPORT_ANCHOR=7`. You can delete them. |

title: Configuration · Models
text: The agent loop in the `agent` container builds its ladder of models from these keys and re-reads them every minute, so a change on Set up, Model reaches the bot within a minute even though `GET /settings` flags them `restart`. The ask pane reads the same keys on every question. title: Configuration · Parent and children
text: A node with a parent posts the hourly means of its own sensors to `PARENT_API_URL/aggregates` and alert timestamps to `PARENT_API_URL/events`, with `PARENT_TOKEN` as Bearer and `NODE_SCALE` as `scale`. Values and times go up; where, what was said and who said it stay. See [Federation](federation.md). | Setting | Default | Values | Meaning | Kind | |---|---|---|---|---| | `PARENT_API_URL` | blank = none | `http://<district>:8080` | The parent node. | runtime · outward | | `PARENT_TOKEN` | blank | string | What this node presents to its parent. | runtime · secret | | `AGGREGATE_TOKEN` | blank | string | What this node demands from its children on `POST /aggregates` and `POST /events`, and all it opens. Without it the node accepts no children (403). | runtime · secret |

Also `/nearby.radius_km`. | | `BAD_MIN_SEPARATION_M` | bali-air-dispatch | `150` | A station closer than this is taken to be the node's own hardware. | | `BAD_EXCLUDE` | bali-air-dispatch | blank | Station ids that are ours and the rules above missed. | | `BAD_INCLUDE_INDOOR` | bali-air-dispatch | `0` | `1` keeps stations the archive suspects are indoors. | | `MAKE_ENABLED` | make | `0` | Off on purpose: the Fab Lab Network directory it reads is not openly licensed. Read [packs/make/README.md](../../packs/make/README.md) first. Needs `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE=1`. | | `MAKE_RADIUS_KM` | make | `50` | How far to look for a fab lab, in km. | | `MAKE_SOURCE` | make | `archive` | `archive` reads the dated monthly snapshots; `live` reads api.fablabs.io, which says it has been removed. | | `MAKE_SNAPSHOT` | make | blank = newest | Pins a snapshot, e.g. `2026.07.31_labs.json`. | | `MAKE_REFRESH_DAYS` | make | `30` | How often to re-read, about 5.3 MB each time. | | `THINGDATA_INSTANCES` | thingdata | blank | ThingData servers, `slug=url`, comma-separated. Masked once saved. | | `SURFACE_HEAT_RING_KM` | surface-heat | `3` | Outer edge of the ring the node's cell is compared with, in km; it starts at 1 km. | | `SURFACE_HEAT_MIN_CLEAR` | surface-heat | `0.5` | The share of cell and ring that must be clear land for a scene to count. | | `TERRAIN_RADIUS_M` | terrain | `5000` | Half-width of the square around the node, in metres. title: Configuration · Known gaps
text: > **Gap in v0.90.0.** `REPORT_DEPTH` is declared, validated and offered in Set up, and nothing reads it. > **Gap in v0.90.0.** Three runtime keys are stored and shown as in force when set from the dashboard, and a reader > ignores the database value. `/presence`, the only reader of `NODE_KIND`, reads the environment. The Reticulum > bridge reads `ACT_TOKEN` and `RETICULUM_ALERT_DESTINATIONS` from its own environment (the app itself does read the > `ACT_TOKEN` override). Set these in `.env` and restart.

title: Configuration · Where this leads
text: The settings that decide what leaves the machine are on [Sharing and security](sharing.md), with what each one sends and how coarse. The sensors the first groups point at are on [Sensors](sensors.md).

title: The dashboard
text: The dashboard is where a household reads its node: what it observed about the place, what it asks of the people there, whether that worked, and what the machine itself is doing. The node computes and the page draws, so every sentence, number and state word on it comes from the node's routes. A number the page worked out for itself would be a bug. The address `/` opens one of three pages: | address | what it opens | |---|---| | `/` | the five doors, Now, Place, Node, Data and Wall, with Set up behind the gear. The default | | `/?layout=mobile` | the phone page, one column. A phone opening `/` is moved here on its own, see [The phone page](#the-phone-page) | | `/?layout=classic` | the classic dashboard, with its ladder, its three modes and its six views, see [The classic dashboard](#the-classic-dashboard) | All three read the same routes with the same token, kept in the browser as `planetai_admin` (the admin token) or `planetai_act` (the token for closing a loop, which can answer the node and change nothing). Every file the pages load, scripts, stylesheets, fonts and the vendored map and drawing libraries, is served by name from `GET /static/{name}`, so the dashboard draws on a network with no route out.

title: The dashboard · A first read
text: 1. **Open it.** `planetai ui` prints the addresses (`On this machine: http://localhost:8080/`, `On your network: http://<ip>:8080/`, and the tailnet address once `planetai mesh` has run) and both tokens. Open one. While the page loads it shows **Asking the node**: each route it asked, with its time in milliseconds or `no answer`. A `no answer` row is the part of the node that is not answering. Nothing on that screen is a reading yet. 2. **Unlock the screen.** At `SHARE_LEVEL=off`, the default, a browser without a token gets "This node is not sharing its readings with this screen." and two fields. Paste the admin token and press **Unlock this screen**. To let every screen in the house read the node without a token, set `SHARE_LEVEL` to `open` in Set up › Sharing (see [Sharing](sharing.md)). 3. **Read Now.** The bar shows the node's name and the five doors. Now opens on the headline issue: its sign, the node's sentence, and its day drawn at every distance against the line. The four distances (house, street, ring, region) follow in one line, each with its provenance word. 4. **Answer what is asked.** If the node is asking something, **What to do** holds a framed card with the action it chose and **Done**, **Not now** and **Doesn't fit**. Press the one that is true. The page says "Recorded.", or for Not now, that the node holds the question for three hours unless it reaches danger. If it says the screen can't answer yet, the screen holds no token: unlock it in Set up › This screen. When nothing is asked the section reads "Nothing is asked now." 5. **Find the record.** Data › Ledger has your answer at the top, with its stage and time. On Node, **What it remembers** keeps the diary and what the node learned about what works here. 6. **Look around.** Place is the ground as a map. Node says whether the machine is working and what leaves it. Wall is the screen for a room, read from three metres.

title: The dashboard · The bar and the foot
