text: ```bash planetai act 12 "read the test alert on my phone" ``` ``` ● recorded: you acted on #12 rho is now <ρ> (<answered>/<asked> alerts answered, median <m> min) ``` Use the alert id the test printed. On a node whose only act-level alert is the test, ρ is now `1.0`, one of one. Write what you did in your own words, because the note is the record. Without one the CLI writes the placeholder `acted`, and the bot and the MCP `act` tool refuse a blank note. **Now there is:** measure. There is a row in `actions` and ρ has a value: every act-level alert answered within 24 hours, over the last 30 days.

title: First ten minutes · 5. Open the dashboard
text: ```bash planetai ui ``` ![The Now door of node #1 in Bali, an evening after a dusty morning](img/now.jpg "Now on node #1: the sentence, the day against the WHO line, the week below it, and what to do.") ``` On this machine: http://localhost:8080/ On your network: http://<lan ip>:8080/ SHARE_LEVEL is off, so a screen on your network gets the dashboard and the node's status and no readings. ``` Below that it prints three tokens and creates the admin and act tokens if they are missing. The admin token is for Set up: "Anyone with it can change what the node reads and where it sends alerts. Treat it like a password." The backup token is read-only, for a NAS. The act token closes a loop from a phone and "cannot read a secret or change a setting". 1. Open `http://localhost:8080/`. At the default `SHARE_LEVEL=off` every browser, including one on the node's own machine, sees the node's name and status and no readings. The page opens on the five doors, Now, Place, Node, Data and Wall, with **Set up** behind the gear. A phone is sent to the phone page. 2. In Set up › This screen, paste the admin token (or the act token, in "Token for closing a loop") and press **Unlock this screen**. The readings appear. 3. With the admin token in, "A phone" shows a QR code. Scan it and the phone page opens holding the act token, so the phone can answer the node with nothing typed. Set up is also where you add sensors (Sources), choose the bot's model (Model) and change any setting without touching `.env`. The classic page, with its Simple, Advanced and Learn modes, is at `/?layout=classic`. See [Dashboard](dashboard.md) and [Sharing](sharing.md). The Place door and the Wall draw streets, buildings and their names once the node holds the map of its place. If you skipped it during install, fetch it now: ```bash planetai run place basemap ``` It cuts OpenStreetMap out of Protomaps' daily build in three rings round the node, down to street level, and adds drone imagery where somebody flew. `build.protomaps.com` and OpenAerialMap learn which square it fetched (`GROUND_RADIUS_KM`, 12 km by default); after that every tile is read from `out/ground/`. `--dry-run` says what it would ask for. Until it has run, `planetai doctor` lists **The map of this place** under what is left to set up. **Now there is:** the loop on a screen, drawn from the node's `GET /issues` document.

title: First ten minutes · When a real alert arrives
text: The test alert belongs to no issue, so it counts in ρ but never shows as an open alert on the page. The first real act-level alert from an air or heat rule does. It closes on the classic page's Now view (`/?layout=classic`); the doors and the phone page draw only an event's card. Until then Decide says "This node sends alerts, not events." and "Nothing is asking for anything." 1. **Read it under Decide**, the first section under the lead. Each open alert has a card with *what was seen*, the alert's first line, and *what this node suggests*, the rule's 👉 recommendation. Press **Decide about this**, fill in "Who is deciding" and "What will be done" (or press **Take its word**), then **Record the decision**. The page confirms the decision and reminds you to press **I did this** when it is done. A decision closes no alert and does not enter ρ; it records that somebody looked. 2. **Record it when it is done.** Press **I did this** on the same card, fill in "Who" and "What you did", then **Record it**. The page answers "Recorded. The node watches what happens next." This needs the act or admin token in the browser; without one the node refuses and the page says where the token comes from. 3. **See it under Measure.** "Whether it worked" shows ρ, answered over asked, and the median minutes from alert to answer, the same figure as the `rho` line of `planetai status`. The funnel counts asked, acknowledged, acted and measured. `measured` goes up 48 hours after the act if the same rule has stayed silent on the same sensor, and "Which of these worked" shows it rule by rule. A node on `ALERT_ENGINE=events` or `shadow` shows one card per open event instead, with the action for the readings as they are now and **Done**, **Not now** and **Doesn't fit**; see [Dashboard](dashboard.md#decide). **Now there is:** the whole loop on one page, and a ledger of who decided and who did what. > **Note.** `DECISION_REQUIRED=1` (Set up → Alerts, off by default) makes the node refuse an act, with HTTP 409, > unless a decision was recorded against the same alert first. It is for a node that acts for a street rather > than a house.

title: First ten minutes · 6. Talk to it
text: ```bash planetai agent local ``` It installs Ollama if it is missing, starts it as a service, and recommends a model without downloading it: ``` ● machine has 16 GB ● no model is on this machine yet, and this command does not fetch one. For 16 GB the recommendation is qwen3.5:9b (6.6 GB on disk, Apache-2.0) Pull it when you want it: planetai agent local pull qwen3.5:9b ``` Under 16 GB the recommendation is `qwen3.5:4b` (3.4 GB). `planetai agent local pull <tag>` downloads it and points `AGENT_MODEL` at it. The command then builds and starts the `agent` container, which answers your Telegram messages with the node's own tools, and ends with "running. Message your bot: is the node healthy? /act 23 closed the windows /model". On Linux it also sets `OLLAMA_URL=http://172.17.0.1:11434` and warns that Ollama must listen on `0.0.0.0` so the container can reach it. `/act 23` with no words gets a question back and records nothing. The local model gets the node's read and act tools, never the admin ones. At the default, `AGENT_PREFER=private`, nothing the bot is asked leaves your network. A bigger model on another machine of yours can sit above the local one on the [model ladder](bot.md) (one at a public address waits, like an online model, for `fallback` or `strongest`), and an online model is used only after someone here chooses `fallback` or `strongest` and sets a key. **Now there is:** an agent on the node, answering from the node's own tools.

title: First ten minutes · Every day
text: ``` planetai status is it alive, what has it read, what fired, ρ planetai doctor every check, with the fix written next to any failure planetai logs what it is doing right now planetai update backup, fetch the latest version, check its signature, migrate, rebuild, verify planetai storage where the data is, where the copies go ``` `planetai doctor` prints one line per check: `✓`, `✗`, or an amber `!` for something worth saying that does not fail the run, such as a new version being out. The fix is under every `✗` and `!`, after a `→`. Below the checks, **Data sources** lists what the node needs for its basic job. It ends with `all good` or `fix the marked lines, then run planetai doctor again`. A node installed from the release tarball also shows `release signature verified on last update`. A good week is a short report a few times a day, a handful of alerts, one or two that changed what you did, and a fresh file in `backups/` every morning. Dozens of alerts a day means the thresholds are wrong for your place. Write to us with which ones instead of raising them: a node that is quiet only because you raised its threshold is lying to you.

title: First ten minutes · When something is off
text: Run `planetai doctor` first, then read [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md), which is ordered by what is on your screen. To ask for help, write to **info@fab.city** with `planetai status`, `planetai doctor` and the last twenty lines of `planetai logs`. Never send `.env`: it holds your tokens.

title: First ten minutes · Where this leads
text: The node now reads models and public stations. The next part is what measures your own place, [Sensors and sources](sensors.md). With sensors indoors and out, a node can answer questions a model cannot. On node #1, three indoor kits and one outdoor kit showed in their first week that the indoor PM2.5 followed the street's, with the house holding back about a third of it, so what the house breathed came in from the street. The `insight` pack's `agreement` rule says this every day, and when the room turns worse than the street the `air-quality` pack's `inside_worse_ventilate` rule says to open a window. After sensors, [the dashboard](dashboard.md) and [the report](report.md) are how you read the node, and [alerts](alerts.md) are how it asks.

title: Grafana
text: The dashboard draws the node the way this project decided to draw it. Grafana is for the person who keeps the node and wants to look at their own data their own way: a month of one room, every sensor on one chart, the hours a sensor went quiet, panels nobody here thought of. It runs beside the dashboard and never replaces it. Grafana reads the database directly, raw readings included, and carries none of the dashboard's rules. It will not mark a number `live`, `partial` or `stale`, and it draws a model's estimate the same way as a measurement unless you tell it apart. The starter dashboard's title says so ("keeper's view · no provenance"), and the [traps](#what-grafana-will-not-tell-you) further down are yours to keep in mind.

title: Grafana · Turn it on
text: ```bash planetai grafana ``` It adds `grafana` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES`, makes Grafana's database login, starts Grafana and prints its address, `http://127.0.0.1:3000` unless you changed it. Sign in as `admin` with `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, or `admin` until you set one. The starter dashboard is in the PLANETAI folder. Grafana listens on the node's own machine only. From a laptop, tunnel to it: ```bash ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 <the node's machine> ``` and open `http://localhost:3000` on the laptop. To open it to the house network instead, set `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD` first, then `GRAFANA_BIND=0.0.0.0`, and run `planetai grafana` again. Whoever signs in sees everything the next section lists. ```bash planetai grafana off ``` stops it, takes it out of `COMPOSE_PROFILES` and drops the database login. Your own dashboards stay in the `grafana` volume, and come back the next time you turn it on. | key | default | what it does | |---|---|---| | `GRAFANA_PORT` | `3000` | the port Grafana answers on | | `GRAFANA_BIND` | `127.0.0.1` | the address it listens on; `0.0.0.0` is every interface | | `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `admin` | the password of Grafana's `admin` login | The three keys are read at start, so they are changed in `.env`, then `planetai grafana` again. Set up › System says whether Grafana is running, at which address, whether its password is set (never the password) and how to open it from a laptop.

title: Grafana · What it can read
text: Grafana signs in to the database as `planetai_grafana`, a login made by `config/grafana/role.sh` each time Grafana starts. It belongs to `planetai_ro`, the role pack rules already run as, which can read every table except `settings` and the household's own (`captures`, `things`, `learnings`, `digests`, `household`), and write none. On top of that: - every session it opens is read-only; - a query stops after 30 seconds, so a wide panel cannot slow the node down; - it holds four connections at most; - its session timezone is the node's `NODE_TZ`, as the app's own connections are; - its password is generated into the `grafana-secret` volume. Nothing goes in `.env`. What it can read is far more than the API gives a screen without a token. The rooms have their real names, the household's sensors stand at their real points, and private channels (a home's counts of what it keeps) are there in full. That is why Grafana listens on loopback by default, and why `GRAFANA_BIND` comes after a password. The tables a panel usually wants are `readings` (`ts, sensor_id, metric, value`), `sensors` (who each sensor is, in which room, and whether it is the household's) and `alert_events` (what the node said and when).

title: Grafana · The starter dashboard
text: It fills itself from this node's sensors: three pickers choose a metric, a room and an outside sensor, out of the ones that reported in the last week. | panel | what it shows | |---|---| | in every room and yard, hourly | the household's own sensors, the hourly mean of the raw readings, mean, max and 95th percentile beside each | | a room by hour of day, one column per day | each cell is one hour's mean. A habit shows as a row, a bad day as a column | | a room against outside | one dot per hour. Above the diagonal the room is worse than outside, so the source is indoors | | when each sensor was heard | every one of the household's sensors, every three hours, red where it sent nothing. A sensor that never spoke is a red row | | outside | every outdoor sensor the node reads, the neighbours' too, and the model, dashed | | radios | how busy each Meshtastic radio's channel is. Empty on a node with no radio | The node's alert events are drawn on the time charts, from when each opened to when it cleared, marked `sent` or `held`. The starter ships with the node and is replaced on every update, so Grafana will not save changes over it. Save as makes a copy that is yours; edit that one.

title: Grafana · What Grafana will not tell you
text: ### The forecast is stored in the future The forecast pack writes each value at the hour it is for, days ahead, as `fc_*` metrics with `fc_lead_hours` beside them. A query with no upper bound, or a time picker set past now, draws tomorrow's forecast as if it had been measured. End every query on `readings` or `readings_1h` with `ts <= now()` (`bucket <= now()` on `readings_1h`). The starter does. ### A silence is drawn as a line Grafana joins the points it has. When a sensor sends nothing for seven hours there are no rows for those hours, so the line runs straight across them. In a time series panel, set *Connect null values* to *Never* and *Insert nulls* to a gap you care about (the starter uses three hours). The heatmap and the when-heard panel show silence without being told. ### Hour of day is the session's Grafana's own axis follows `NODE_TZ`. Inside SQL, use `ts AT TIME ZONE current_setting('TimeZone')`, which is `NODE_TZ` for `planetai_grafana`. The same query pasted into `psql` runs in UTC, eight hours off in Bali, unless you `SET TIME ZONE` first. ### Some rows are models `sensors.kind` says what a row is: `sensor` measured it, `model` estimated it (the CAMS point, Open-Meteo, the forecast), `map` counted it from OpenStreetMap or satellite. `sensors.local` is true for the household's own; the rest are other people's stations the node reads. ### `$__timeGroup` is a number For PostgreSQL it gives epoch seconds, not a timestamp, so it will not join a `generate_series` of times. Wrap it in `to_timestamp(...)`, or build the bucket yourself as the when-heard panel does. ### Names change A room renamed in Set up is renamed in `sensors`. An alert written before that keeps the old name in its text. Next, [Schema](schema.md): every table and view a panel can be built from.

title: How it works
text: A node is two containers on one machine. `db` is Postgres with PostGIS, reachable only from the machine itself. `app` is one Python process that answers the HTTP API on port 8080 and runs eleven loops in the background, a twelfth when the Reticulum bridge is on. Five more containers are optional: the Mosquitto broker for radios and DIY sensors, the `agent` container for the Telegram bot, the Reticulum bridge, an IPFS node for the export and Grafana, with a one-shot `grafana-role` that makes its login. Everything a node does is one of those loops or one of the API's answers, and this page follows a reading through all of it. ![The containers on the machine, and what they reach outside](img/containers.svg "The app and the database always run; the dashed containers run only when their profile is on.")

title: How it works · Sense, then one loop in four stages
text: ``` SENSE adapters: your sensors · other people's stations · open data · Earth models │ (ts, sensor_id, metric, value) ▼ OBSERVE ──▶ DECIDE ──▶ ACT ──▶ MEASURE ──▶ OBSERVE … what is read what to do what has been whether it worked, about this about it asked, of whom and how long it took place ``` `ARCHITECTURE.md` describes three layers, Sense, Observe and Act, measured against the Fab City Index. The dashboard, the four-sentence digest in `GET /issues` and `docs/GUI.md` split the same machinery into the four stages above, and every section on the page belongs to one of them. ### Sense Every adapter (a Smart Citizen kit, the ring of Bali Air Dispatch stations, a CKAN portal, the Copernicus model sampled at your coordinates, a pack's own `adapter.py`) returns the same two things: a list of sensors and a list of readings `(ts, sensor_id, metric, value)`. The poll loop asks every enabled adapter every `POLL_SECONDS` (300) and upserts what comes back. The core does not know what `pm25` means. It stores rows, and each sensor row says how its number was produced (`kind`), whether it is yours and within `LOCAL_RADIUS_M` (500 m) of the node (`local`), and whether it may be counted (`custody`). See [Concepts](concepts.md). ### Observe Readings land in one table, and three views do the arithmetic. `stats` holds the last 24 hours per sensor and metric (15-minute, hourly and 24-hour means, and how long a sensor has been silent), `readings_1h` holds hourly means over all history, and `observations` holds the latest value from every slow source: a portal, a model, a map. On top of them, `GET /issues` is the one document the dashboard draws. For every issue the keeper declared in `NODE_ISSUES` it computes a state, the four distances with their provenance, a sentence in English, Bahasa Indonesia and Spanish, the open alerts and a 24-hour series. It also names a headline issue and writes a digest of four sentences, one per stage. Two more reads sit beside it. `GET /shape` is "the day this place usually has", indoor against outdoor, hour by hour; it needs 7 days of the node's own readings for a day, 14 for a week, 60 for a month and 365 for a year. `GET /reach` says how far back each kind of source can be asked. Every node exposes the same read [API](api.md), and the dashboard, the CLI, the bot and a NAS are all clients of it. ### Decide On the page, Decide is "what to do about it", the first section under the lead on Now. It draws a card for each issue with an open act-level alert, showing what was seen and "what this node suggests", which is the rule's own last line when that line begins with 👉. A node running the event engine draws one card per open event instead, with the action for the readings as they are now and three answers. A person may record a decision on an alert's card. It is written to `actions` with `stage: decided`, and it moves nothing: it closes no alert, it is not in ρ and it is not a stage in the funnel. `ARCHITECTURE.md` maps decide to the `acknowledged` row of its ledger; the page's `decided` row is a separate record. With `DECISION_REQUIRED=1` (off by default) the node refuses an `acted` with HTTP 409 unless a `decided` row exists for the same alert, whichever way the act arrives. ### Act A rule is SQL that returns rows, plus a message template, a level and a cooldown. The rules loop runs every rule once a minute as the read-only role `planetai_ro`, and every row that comes back is a candidate alert. A cooldown per rule and sensor stops it repeating, the level decides whether it interrupts anyone, and quiet hours hold everything but `act`. The alert goes out on [Telegram](channels.md), the LoRa mesh, LXMF and Home Assistant. When a person does something about it, that is a row in `actions`, and it can come from five places: the dashboard's **I did this** (which needs `ACT_TOKEN` or `ADMIN_TOKEN` in the browser), `planetai act`, `/act <id> <what you did>` in Telegram, the MCP `act` tool, or an `act <id>` message over Reticulum. An agent drafts and never dispatches, so nothing is recorded as done without that row. A rule that declares a `kind` (the heat and air-quality rules do) takes another path when `ALERT_ENGINE` is `shadow` or `events`: its rows are folded into one [alert event](concepts.md#rules-alerts-actions) per issue per house. In `shadow` the engine records what it would send and sends nothing. In `events` it sends that one message, only danger in quiet hours and at most `ALERT_MAX_PER_DAY` (4) pushes a day outside danger, and the old heat and air rules stop sending. The default, `rules`, runs no engine. See [Alerts](alerts.md). ### Measure [ρ](rho.md) is the share of act-level asks in the last 30 days that had an `acknowledged` or `acted` row within 24 hours. An ask is an alert that was sent, or an event the engine sent at act level, and a node pools its children's alert timestamps with its own. It is the core's own Index cell, `Governance|<Scale>`. Only the node that sends the alert also receives the answer, so only a node can measure it. Beside ρ the funnel counts the same alerts four times: asked, acknowledged, acted, measured. Nothing posts `measured`. The node derives it: an act followed by 2,880 minutes (48 hours) of silence from the same rule on the same sensor, counted only for rules the node still runs. `GET /effect` asks the same question per rule over the whole record, how many acts and how many cleared, and gives a recovery time in hours only for a rule that declares `watch: {metric, over}`. Four do, two in the air-quality pack and two in heat. A pack's `cells.yml` computes the other Index cells the node has the data to fill, each with a state; see [Concepts](concepts.md#the-index-and-its-cells).

title: How it works · The loops
text: | loop | every | what it does | |---|---|---| | poll | `POLL_SECONDS` (300) | asks every enabled adapter for sensors and readings and upserts them; a source that fails leaves its error in `/health.last_error`, and a loop that fails outright appears under its name in `/health.errors` | | rules and report | 60 s | writes the [report](report.md) if its hour is due, then runs every rule as `planetai_ro` | | hourly means | hourly | fills `readings_1h_done` with the finished hours, the last 26 every hour and all of them on the first run after a start and of each local day; `readings_1h` reads it | | usual for the hour | hourly | rebuilds `usual_by_hour`, each room's usual for each local hour over the fourteen complete days before today, which the event rules read | | push aggregates | hourly | if `PARENT_API_URL` is set, posts the last two hours of hourly means to the parent's `/aggregates` | | push events | hourly | if `PARENT_API_URL` is set, posts this node's alert timestamps of the last 36 hours to the parent's `/events` | | release check | hourly | unless `UPDATE_CHECK=off`, asks planetai.fab.city which version is current and says so in `/health`, the page's top bar and once per version on Telegram. It installs nothing | | node list | hourly | unless `UPDATE_CHECK=off`, reads the programme's `registry.json` from GitHub and serves it at `/nodes`, each other node's point to one decimal and no contact | | introduced species | hourly | only with the `eyes` pack on and `SPECIES_MATCH=on`: once a week reads the country's GRIIS checklist from GBIF | | others' records | hourly | only with the `eyes` pack on and `SPECIES_MATCH=on`: once a week counts GBIF's open records in each of the node's seven res-8 cells | | what the house learned | hourly | once a local day, in its first hour: what worked, what is usual, the alerts that may not fit, and the diary's entries | | Reticulum | 300 s | only with `RETICULUM_URL` set: asks the bridge for its health and the peers it has heard, for `/health.reticulum`. The bridge itself turns an `act <id>` message into `POST /actions` | With `MQTT_HOST` set, one more thread subscribes to the broker for Meshtastic radios, DIY sensors and the topics a loaded pack's `hooks.py` names in `MQTT_TOPICS` (the `smartcitizen` pack's `device/sck/#`). That pack passes the messages of the devices listed in `SC_FORWARD` on to smartcitizen.me unchanged, on a thread of its own, and with `HA_DISCOVERY=1` the `home-assistant` pack publishes discovery entities after every batch of readings. Every document the node sends or serves as a contract carries a `schema` key: `issues-v0`, `days-v0`, `export-v0`, `report-v0`, and the two pushes, `aggregates-v0` and `events-v0`. See [Federation](federation.md).

title: How it works · One shape at every scale
text: The same code and the same contracts run at a house that polls its devices, at a lab that also watches its city's open-data portal, and anywhere a global model can be sampled. What differs is the `kind` of each source and the `scale` the node declares: | `sensors.kind` | what it is | cadence | lands in | |---|---|---|---| | `sensor` | a device on your LAN, or a nearby public one | minutes | `stats` | | `portal` | an open-data or statistical API | days to months | `observations` | | `model` | a global model sampled at a point | hours | `observations` | | `map` | what is around the node, from OpenStreetMap | monthly | `observations` and PostGIS tables | | `child` | a node below this one, pushing hourly means | hourly | `readings`, as `<child>/<sensor_id>` | | `peer` | another node whose numbers are shown, never counted | none | display only | | `facility` | a named place with a point and no readings, such as a fab lab from the `make` pack | monthly | `sensors` only | Index cells roll up only as far as Region; [Concepts](concepts.md#the-index-and-its-cells) has what a cell needs at each scale. The node also carries a pinned snapshot of the source registry, served at `/sources`; see [The source registry](sources.md).

title: How it works · What leaves the machine, and what never does
text: Raw readings stay. What travels is a summary: hourly means and alert timestamps to a parent node, if `PARENT_API_URL` names one; the daily [export](storage.md), with hourly means, your own sensors named by role (`indoor-1`, `outdoor-2`), the Index cells, each alert's first line, ρ, the household's offers and its res-8 cell's centre, never its point, under CC BY 4.0. The export is readable at every [sharing level](sharing.md). ![What leaves the machine, to whom, and which are off by default](img/what-leaves.svg "Raw readings stay. A dashed line leaves only when somebody here turns it on.") Exact coordinates and a household's own sentences never leave in a push or the export. The events push carries rule, level and timestamps, and no alert text, actor, note or sensor id. Your own sensor ids leave only in the hourly means pushed to a parent you chose. Nothing finer than the node's resolution-8 cell (about 500 m to an edge) reaches a reader the node does not know: `/health`, `/export`, and the household's own sensors in `/sensors` and `/stats` give the centre of that cell, and only this machine or a token gets three decimals. The shape of the building behind `/place/geojson` needs a token at every sharing level. Alerts go out on the channels you connect, so an alert sent by Telegram passes through Telegram's servers. Every hour the node asks planetai.fab.city which version is current and reads the programme's list of nodes from GitHub. Neither request carries anything about the house, but each shows the house's internet address to the host it asks; `UPDATE_CHECK=off` in Set up → Sharing stops both. Everything else leaves only when somebody here turns it on: | what | when | what the other side learns | |---|---|---| | Reticulum presence | `RETICULUM_PRESENCE=1` | a coarse H3 cell, resolution 3 by default and never finer than 6 | | live map tiles | `MAP_TILES=on` | which square of the planet the browser showing the dashboard is looking at, at resolution 8 and coarser | | an online model | `AGENT_PREFER` is `fallback` or `strongest` and an online key is set | the question asked of the bot or the ask pane, and the node's answers to the model's tool calls. At the default, `private`, both use a model on this machine or your own network | | species names | Name species with GBIF (`SPECIES_MATCH=on`) | a finding's scientific name; the weekly reads tell GBIF the country and the shapes of the seven cells | | offers | the household marks a thing to lend or give | its class, name, condition and count at the node's cell, public at `GET /offers` and in the export | | a detailed basemap | somebody types `planetai run place basemap` or `planetai run earth-engine basemap` | Protomaps, OpenAerialMap or Earth Engine learn once which square the node is in; after that the map is read from the node | | Smart Citizen forwarding | a device token listed in `SC_FORWARD` | smartcitizen.me gets that device's messages exactly as the device sent them | | IPFS | `IPFS_PUBLISH=1` (`planetai ipfs` sets it and starts the container) | the daily export, added to IPFS; never the dump | | an off-machine backup | `BACKUP_REMOTE` names an rclone remote | the whole backup, the database dump included, goes to the remote you named |

title: How it works · Where the decisions live
text: | decision | where | |---|---| | what a metric means, thresholds, messages | a pack's `rules.yml`; see [Packs](packs.md) | | which cells the node fills | a pack's `cells.yml` | | what a metric *is*: ambient, the box, battery, derived | `channels.yml`, core and per pack | | what a place watches, and in which order | `NODE_ISSUES`, declared in each pack's `issue.yml`; see [Issues](issues.md) | | how the node speaks | `ALERT_LOCALE`, `ALERT_LEVEL`, `QUIET_*`, `REPORT_*`; see [Configuration](configuration.md) | | whether an act needs a decision first | `DECISION_REQUIRED` (default `0`) | | whether heat and air alerts are sent as events | `ALERT_ENGINE` (`rules`, `shadow` or `events`; default `rules`) | | how much of the page opens, and in what order | `UI_MODE` (`simple`, `advanced`, `learn`) and `UI_LAYOUT` | | whether the page may fetch live tiles | `MAP_TILES` (default `off`) | | whether the ground is a drawing or a map that pans and zooms | `UI_GROUND` (`svg` or `map`; default `svg`) | | whether the node asks which version is current | `UPDATE_CHECK` (default `on`) | | whether the bot and the ask pane may use an online model | `AGENT_PREFER` (default `private`) | | whether the node names the nearest fab lab | `MAKE_ENABLED` (default `0`) | | who may read it | `SHARE_LEVEL` and the tokens; see [Sharing and security](sharing.md) | | what is retired and when it returns | [`SPEC.md`](spec.md) §6 |

title: How it works · Refusals that hold at every stage
text: No raw readings leave the instance that recorded them. No cell is upgraded from `mock` or `partial` to `live` by aggregation. No agent dispatches without a human row in `actions`. No layer requires a cloud provider to function. No scale is skipped: a city aggregator is built from nodes, not declared from above. The longer form, with the staging from one node to a bioregion, is [Architecture](architecture.md). > **Gap in v0.90.0.** Some of that staging is not built. The Act layer in `ARCHITECTURE.md` ends in a > fabrication ticket when a decision is physical; there is no such ticket and no `fabricate` stage, and no job > has been handed to a workshop. The `make` pack, off until `MAKE_ENABLED=1`, only names the nearest fab lab. > Nodes finding each other (`docs/SPEC_discovery.md`) is not built. A node as a key rather than a name > (`docs/SPEC_identity.md`) and the second ρ, which would ask whether the reading recovered > (`docs/SPEC_rho.md`), are Phase 1 with nothing built. A decision on the dashboard is one person deciding for > one node; how several households' decisions become a street's is not on a node at all.

title: How it works · Where this leads
text: The words this page used, `custody`, `kind`, the four distances, the H3 cell, are defined in [Concepts](concepts.md). To run the loop yourself, [install](install.md) a node and spend the [first ten minutes](first-ten-minutes.md) closing one.

title: Install
text: This page puts the node itself on a machine: two containers, a database on this disk, and the loops that read your place every five minutes. Once it is done the node has pulled the air model and the climate normals for your coordinates, answers on port 8080, and keeps every reading it takes on this machine. Nothing has reached a phone yet; that is the [next page](first-ten-minutes.md). > **The short way.** Six commands, in order, each one waiting for the one before: > 1. `curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/preflight | bash` checks the machine. > 2. `curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/install | bash` asks four questions and installs the node. Near the end it > offers to fetch the map of your place; say `y`, or run `planetai run place basemap` later. > 3. `planetai doctor` shows every check, and under **Data sources** what is left, each with its fix. If the > terminal says `planetai: command not found`, open a new one: the installer adds the command to the PATH of > new terminals. > 4. `planetai telegram` connects your phone. > 5. `planetai test-alert` sends a real alert. > 6. `planetai act <id>` answers it, and the loop is closed. > > The rest of this page and the [next](first-ten-minutes.md) explain each step.

title: Install · 1. Check the machine
text: ```bash curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/preflight | bash ``` It reads the machine in a few seconds and installs nothing. It prints one table, a row each for OS, architecture, memory, free disk, container runtime, whether the disk can be written, `python3`, egress and ports, and every failing row carries the command that fixes it on that machine. The last line and the exit code are the verdict: | exit | verdict line | what to do | |---|---|---| | `0` | `This machine can run a node.` | install | | `1` | `<N> checks failed. Each line above carries the fix. Nothing was installed.` | fix the named rows and run it again | | `2` | `No container runtime can be installed on <OS>.` | the OS is below every runtime's floor; the preflight prints two routes, Linux in a virtual machine or Linux on the metal ([Platforms](platforms.md), [Revive a laptop](revive-a-laptop.md)) | Never continue past `2`. The node needs 4 GB of memory (8 GB under WSL2) and 3 GB of free disk. The installer runs the same preflight first and stops on `1`; on `2` it prints the verdict and exits without an error, because that is an answer.

title: Install · 2. Run the install line
text: ```bash curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/install | bash ``` `/install` is a small stub. It looks up the released version and fetches the `install` script, and the preflight, from exactly that commit, so everything you receive belongs to one release. The script prints the logo with the published version under it, runs the preflight, downloads the node's tarball from `planetai.fab.city/node0/get`, checks its checksum and its signature, unpacks it into `~/planetai` keeping any `.env` already there, links the command to `~/.local/bin/planetai`, and hands over to `planetai setup`. Before the questions the screen shows: ``` >> downloading the node from https://planetai.fab.city/node0 >> checksum verified >> signature verified ``` If either check fails it stops before anything is unpacked. What each refusal says, and why the answer is to stop, is on [Updating](updating.md#updates-are-signed). To put a second node somewhere else on the same machine: ```bash PLANETAI_HOME=~/somewhere bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/node0/install)" ```

title: Install · 3. Answer the four questions
text: `planetai setup` opens with **Let's set up a node.** and asks: | | question | what it writes | |---|---|---| | 1 | A short name for this node (lowercase, dashes). The default is the hostname. | `NODE_NAME` | | 2 | Where is it? Type a neighbourhood, town or city. It asks OpenStreetMap's Nominatim and Open-Meteo, lists the hits with their time zone, and asks `Is that the right place?` even when there is one. The list ends with a choice to type the place differently; if nothing matches, paste `lat,lon`. | `NODE_LAT`, `NODE_LON`, `NODE_TZ`, `NODE_CITY` | | 3 | What is this node for? A home, a business, a community or lab node, or a district or region node. | `NODE_KIND`; a district also sets `NODE_SCALE=city` | | 4 | Do you have a sensor? None yet, or a Smart Citizen kit, which asks for the kit number from its smartcitizen.me URL. | `SC_DEVICES` | After the place, one line says what the node will use as its outdoor reference. Inside Bali it is the island's public stations, the `bali-air-dispatch` pack, which the Bali preset turns on; everywhere else it is the global CAMS model at your coordinates, with no key. A place inside Bali, Barcelona, Boston or Santiago also takes that pilot's preset and files the node under the pilot's city key. Then **Here's the plan** lists the name, place, time zone, city key, sensor and outdoor reference, and asks `Install with these?`. Saying no changes nothing. Saying yes writes the answers to `.env` first, so a failure later keeps them for the next run, and starts the seven steps below. The place is the answer that matters most: it fixes the H3 cell the node stands in and the 500 m radius inside which a sensor counts as this node's own. Without a sensor the node still knows your weather, the satellite air model for your district and forty years of climate for your coordinates; see [Before a sensor](before-a-sensor.md). > **Only Smart Citizen, for now.** The installer offers one kit. AirGradient and PurpleAir are read by their own > packs, `airgradient` and `purpleair`, each on once `AIRGRADIENT_HOSTS` or `PURPLEAIR_HOSTS` is set in Set up › > Sources. Details on the [sensors](sensors.md) page. ### Without a terminal An agent, CI or a provisioning script installs from a file. With no terminal, `planetai setup` prints this example itself: ```bash cat > node.json <<'JSON' {"name": "my-node", "place": "Palma de Mallorca", "kind": "home", "sensor": {}} JSON planetai setup --answers node.json ``` `place` is geocoded with Open-Meteo, first hit, or replaced by `"lat"` and `"lon"`. `kind` is `home` (the default), `business`, `community` or `district`. `sensor` is `{}` or one of `{"sc": "19880"}`, `{"sc_user": "name"}`, `{"airgradient": "host"}`, `{"purpleair": "ip"}`; the last two set `AIRGRADIENT_HOSTS` and `PURPLEAIR_HOSTS`. The answers become `install.sh` flags and the installer runs with `--yes`. It needs `python3`, standard library only, and ends with `installed. planetai status --json for the state; planetai ui for the token.`

title: Install · What the installer does
text: It announces seven steps, and each one prints its elapsed time and a heartbeat at least every ten seconds. The full log is in `.planetai-install.log`. 1. **Container runtime.** Detects OrbStack, Docker Desktop, Colima or a systemd Docker and starts it. On Linux without Docker it installs it: `pacman` on Arch; Docker's own Ubuntu repository on an Ubuntu derivative such as Mint or Pop!_OS, because Docker's script misreads those as Debian; `get.docker.com` everywhere else, plain Ubuntu included. It tells a daemon that is down apart from a socket you may not use yet, and carries on under the new `docker` group without asking you to log out. With Podman and no Docker it installs nothing and stops, printing the three lines that let Podman answer to `docker` (`podman-docker`, the user `podman.socket`, and `DOCKER_HOST`). No node has run on Podman yet. 2. **`.env`.** Copies `.env.example` (mode 600), applies the pilot preset if any, writes the answers, stamps `NODE_VERSION`, and generates `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `ADMIN_TOKEN`. It refuses to start without coordinates, and refuses a new database password over a database volume an earlier node left behind. 3. **Port and folders.** Checks that `APP_PORT` (8080) is free, and creates `backups`, `exports` and `out`. 4. **The database image.** Pulls `imresamu/postgis:16-3.4-alpine` (about 162 MB, amd64 and arm64) with visible progress. 5. **Build and start.** `docker compose up -d --build`: the `app` image on `python:3.12-slim`, then both containers. 6. **Schema.** Waits for Postgres and applies `init.sql`, the whole schema, idempotent, the same file a fresh volume and an update both run. 7. **Checks.** Modules in the image, database healthy, app answering, `backup.sh` executable. Then it adds the nightly backup to your crontab (`17 3 * * *`). Unless `--no-bootstrap` was given, the first start pulls about 4,500 rows of history for your coordinates: 92 days of hourly PM2.5 and PM10 from the Copernicus air model, and NASA POWER's monthly normals, so `planetai status` has something to say within minutes. The installer ends with one line you can paste into an issue, starting `install OK`, with the node's name, how long the seven steps took and the port.

title: Install · When it finishes
text: `planetai setup` restarts the app with your settings and runs the [doctor](cli.md). A cross next to *database answers* or *node answers on :8080* means something is wrong; see [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). Below the checks the doctor lists the node's **Data sources** and ends with **To finish setting up**: what is still missing, most important first, each with the one thing to do. On a new node without a sensor, *Add your sensor* comes first, with the address of the Set up page, and then: ``` To finish setting up 1. Connect Telegram, two minutes: planetai telegram 2. No backup yet. One runs every night at 03:17; to have one now: planetai backup 3. No map yet. Fetch it once, a few minutes: planetai run place basemap. build.protomaps.com and OpenAerialMap learn roughly where this node is (the square fetched); after that nothing is sent. ``` The weather and satellite models show a dash until the node's first poll, a few minutes after it starts. Without a map yet, setup then offers **The map of this place**: OpenStreetMap streets, buildings and names, and drone imagery where somebody flew, fetched once onto the node (up to tens of MB) and read from `out/ground/` after that. It says first that build.protomaps.com and OpenAerialMap learn the squares within `GROUND_RADIUS_KM` (12 km) of the node. `y` fetches it; Enter leaves it for later. The Place door and the Wall draw no streets without it. The last screen is a box reading **● Your node is running.**, the dashboard's address on this machine and from your phone on the same WiFi, and the settings token (`planetai ui` shows it again), then `What now? [o] open the dashboard [t] connect Telegram [Enter] stay in the terminal`. Run `./install.sh` on its own, or `planetai update`, and it ends with the same doctor and map offer; with `--yes` or no terminal it only prints.

title: Install · Re-running it
text: `~/planetai` with a `VERSION` file or a git checkout is an existing node, and the installer treats a re-run as an update that keeps your `.env`. `planetai setup` on an existing node offers to update it, reconfigure it, make sure it is running, or remove it. If an earlier setup stopped before the containers existed, it says `A set-up here did not finish, but your answers were saved.` and offers to continue with them. To start over, remove first: ```bash planetai remove # containers, database, folder, cron entry, the command itself; asks twice planetai remove --keep-data # the same, but the readings stay in their volume ``` The Docker volume outlives the folder, and every node's compose project is `planetai`, so a fresh install finds the old database; the installer then refuses to give it a new password and names the two ways out ([Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)). `planetai remove` deletes the volumes by name and then checks. If the node will not start at all, `curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/remove | bash -s -- --purge` finds the containers, the four volumes, the folder, the symlink and the crontab line without running any of the node's own code.

title: Install · Where things are
text: ``` ~/planetai/ .env every setting; mode 600; never committed, never pasted backups/ nightly pg_dump, kept BACKUP_KEEP days exports/<node>/ the daily CC BY 4.0 export, one JSON a day out/ what pack scripts write: land-change maps, timelapses, mapping briefs, the kept map (out/ground/) out/captures/ the household's pictures, unless CAPTURES_DIR says elsewhere packs/ the rules; add a folder to add a domain config/rules.yml the two domain-blind core rules and trust's three data/ the pinned source registry and the platform floors, mounted read-only .planetai-release signed or unsigned, and when, for the last install or update .planetai-setup.log what setup and the CLI did .planetai-update.log what the last update did ~/.local/bin/planetai the command ```

title: Install · Machines that stay on
text: A node wants a computer that boots and logs in on its own after a power cut. An x86 Linux box first: a mini PC, or an old laptop with Linux on it, which is often faster than the mini PC you would otherwise buy. A Mac works ([Mac mini](mac-mini.md) has the settings that stop it sleeping), and on Apple Silicon the database runs natively. Windows through WSL2. A Raspberry Pi passes the preflight, and its architecture row says it is untested on hardware. Nobody has run a node on a Pi, a Jetson or a reComputer yet, and `docs/ARM64.md` is the test plan for whoever goes first. The floors, and where each number comes from, are on [Platforms](platforms.md).

title: Install · Where this leads
text: The node is reading. Next, give it a way to reach you and prove the whole path once: [First ten minutes](first-ten-minutes.md).

title: Introduction
text: PLANETAI is hyperlocal compute and intelligence for distributed production, and a node is its unit: one computer per place, on hardware the place already owns. It reads your own sensors and the public stations and models around them, tells the people there in plain sentences what to do, records what they did and measures whether it worked. Raw readings stay on the machine that recorded them. ```bash curl -fsSL https://planetai.fab.city/install | bash ``` The installer asks four questions and has the node running in about two minutes. After that, `planetai telegram` connects the alerts to your phone and `planetai ui` opens the dashboard. [Install](install.md) walks through it, and [First ten minutes](first-ten-minutes.md) takes you from a running node to a closed loop. > **Note.** The node is beta. `main` is the beta channel and every update is signed, but installing one makes you > part of an experiment: things will break, and what you report decides what gets fixed first. Write to > **info@fab.city** with what broke and what helped. We run node #1, `bayu-ungasan`, in Kuta Selatan, Bali, and > node #2 runs in Menorca.

title: Introduction · What it is for
text: Fab labs and makerspaces have spent twenty years building a distributed infrastructure for making things, and since 2014 the cities of the Fab City pledge have committed to producing half of what they consume by 2054. That infrastructure never had computing of its own, a machine at each place that reads the place, works out what it needs and says why it should be made there instead of shipped in. A node is that machine. Its purpose is fixed: clean air, water and soil for the people and the other living things around each node. The rule it runs on is Fab City's rule for production, applied to data. Fab City calls the old pattern PITO, product in, trash out, and the one it builds DIDO, data in, data out: materials stay in the city and knowledge moves between cities. On a node, raw readings stay on the machine and only summaries travel: to a parent node if you name one, into the daily open export, and from one city node per pilot to the [Fab City Index](https://index.fab.city). Today a node reads air and heat from the sensors in and around the house, and land and coast from public and satellite sources. Two packs you turn on yourself read nearby fires and the ground's surface heat from satellites, and a third, `terrain`, says where the next day's rain goes on the ground around the node. Soil has no pack yet. The `make` pack names the nearest fab lab in a sentence, and no node has handed a job to a workshop yet. What runs is the loop from a reading to a person acting and a measured result; the loop from a reading to something made nearby is the direction. [How it works](how-it-works.md#refusals-that-hold-at-every-stage) lists what the canon describes and the code does not have. The programme behind it is at [planetai.fab.city](https://planetai.fab.city/).

title: Introduction · The loop
text: Sensors, public stations, open-data portals and Earth models feed the node. Everything after that is one loop in four stages, observe, decide, act and measure, and the dashboard has a part for each. An alert says what is happening, what it means and what to do. A person answers it on the dashboard, in Telegram or from the terminal, and the node counts how many act-level alerts were answered. That share is [ρ](rho.md), and it can only be measured where the alert is sent and the answer comes back. [How it works](how-it-works.md) follows one reading through every stage. ![Sense feeds observe, decide, act and measure; an act-level alert sent and the answer that comes back are what ρ counts](img/loop.svg "Every act-level alert sent, and every answer that comes back within 24 hours, is what ρ counts.") In learn mode the dashboard puts a question mark on each part of the page that quotes these pages for it, and the [ask pane](ask.md) answers questions about what the page shows, with a model on this machine or your own network unless someone here chooses an online one.

title: Introduction · What stays, and what goes up
text: Raw readings stay on the machine. A parent node, if you name one, gets hourly means and alert timestamps, and the daily open export carries hourly means, the Index cells, the first line of each alert and ρ under CC BY 4.0. By default no question goes to a model outside your network (`AGENT_PREFER=private`) and the dashboard fetches no live map tiles (`MAP_TILES=off`). Every hour the node asks planetai.fab.city whether a newer version is out and reads the programme's list of nodes from GitHub; both show the house's internet address and nothing else, and `UPDATE_CHECK=off` stops both. The full list is in [How it works](how-it-works.md#what-leaves-the-machine-and-what-never-does).

title: Introduction · What a node is not
text: It sends no raw reading anywhere, and it switches nothing on or off; connect it to Home Assistant for that. It does not act for you: an agent may draft, but every act is a person's row in the `actions` table. Low-cost sensors drift and disagree, so it does not replace a reference instrument, and the node says so where it matters. It is also not a cloud service. It is two containers on a machine you own, with the database on a local disk, and the internet is only how it reaches public stations, models and Telegram.

title: Introduction · Who it is for
text: A household with a sensor in the living room that still does not know whether to open the window. A fab lab that wants its own address on the [Fab City Index](https://index.fab.city). A school or clinic with a duty of care. A banjar or a desa that wants its own number on the island's map. And the people who keep the sensors alive for all of them, which [`PRODUCT.md`](../../PRODUCT.md) describes as "someone whose job it is to keep the sensor alive and the alerts correct".

title: MCP server and tools
text: This is the surface an agent holds. Any client that speaks MCP can read what the node read, ask how the place is doing in the household's own words, and record that somebody acted, in that person's words. Nothing an agent does through it takes a reading off the machine. `app/agent.py` mounts it on the API at `/mcp`, streamable HTTP, with twenty-one tools over the node's own endpoints. The tools call the API back on `127.0.0.1`, so they arrive as loopback; `report_now`, `settings_set`, `report_bundle` and `learned` also carry the admin token. The same tools serve Claude Desktop or Claude Code on a laptop across the tailnet, the household's own model on Telegram, the dashboard's ask pane and any other MCP client.

title: MCP server and tools · Connecting
text: ```bash planetai agent ``` prints the tools by class, the endpoint on this machine (`http://localhost:8080/mcp`) and on the tailnet (`http://<MESH_NAME>:8080/mcp`, the MagicDNS name `planetai mesh` records), the header every call must carry, `Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>`, and a block to paste into a client: ```json {"mcpServers": {"planetai-bayu-ungasan": {"type": "http", "url": "http://bayu-ungasan:8080/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>", "X-Agent": "kitchen-claude"}}}} ``` The `X-Agent` value is only a label, put your agent's own name there. [Bring your own agent](agents.md) goes through it step by step with Claude Desktop, up to the first row an agent writes. For Claude Code in a clone of the repository, `.mcp.json` is already there and reads its values from the shell: `PLANETAI_MCP_URL` (default `http://localhost:8080/mcp`), `PLANETAI_ADMIN_TOKEN` and `PLANETAI_AGENT_NAME`, so nothing secret is in the file. From anywhere else: ```bash claude mcp add --transport http planetai "$PLANETAI_MCP_URL" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $PLANETAI_ADMIN_TOKEN" --header "X-Agent: $PLANETAI_AGENT_NAME" ``` Cursor does not expand `${VAR:-default}`, so paste the block from `planetai agent` instead. A local Ollama with an MCP client (mcphost, oterm) uses the same URL on localhost. The whole of `/mcp` needs the admin token and nothing else, whatever `SHARE_LEVEL` says. A missing or wrong token gets `401 {"error": "the agent surface needs Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>"}`. DNS-rebinding protection is off, because the node is reached by LAN IP, `.local` name and tailnet name, so the Host header is not checked and the token is the only gate. Reach it over the tailnet and never with a port forward.

title: MCP server and tools · Read, act, admin
text: Every tool has one class, set in `app/tool_classes.py`: | class | means | tools | |---|---|---| | `read` | asks the node a question; nothing changes | `status`, `health_check`, `sensors`, `context`, `readings`, `report_latest`, `report_bundle`, `history`, `alerts`, `settings_get`, `packs`, `cells`, `issues`, `series`, `export_day`, `learned` | | `act` | records that a person did something, in their own words | `act` | | `admin` | changes the node, runs code on it, or makes it speak to the household unprompted | `settings_set`, `run_pack_script`, `maintenance`, `report_now` | A remote agent, driven by a person, has all twenty-one. The household's own model on the node gets the 17 `read` and `act` tools and nothing else ([the bot](bot.md)). The dashboard's ask pane gets fewer still and runs only reads ([Ask the node](ask.md)). Four tools write: `act`, `report_now`, `settings_set` and `run_pack_script`. `maintenance` is `admin` but writes nothing, it answers with a command for a person to run.

title: MCP server and tools · The tools
text: Start with `health_check`, then `status`. | tool | arguments | returns | |---|---|---| | `status` | none | node, version, schema, uptime, last poll, readings ingested, polls, per-loop errors, mesh, ρ (the `/rho` body), whether the last backup succeeded | | `health_check` | none | `{ok, checks: [{check, ok, fix}]}`: polled in the last 15 minutes; no source errors; a backup in the last two days; no local sensor's ambient channel frozen; with a broker, LoRa radios heard in the last hour. Every failing check names its fix. Also `sources`, the fundamental sources from [`GET /health/sources`](api.md), each with its state and, when not running, its fix; they never make `ok` false | | `issues` | `issue?` | the whole `/issues` object (the issues, `headline` and `headline_rule`, `labels`, `stations` and `stations_silent`, `metrics`, the `asks` ledger, `lead`, the `digest` with its four sentences, `simple` and `prompts`, `geometry`, the packs' `sections`, the alert `events`, each saying with `asking` whether it still asks), or one issue with `as_of` and `labels`: state, the four distances with provenance, the sentence, the open asks | | `sensors` | none | one row per sensor from `/stats`: local, indoor, kind, the 15-minute mean per metric, minutes silent; local first | | `context` | none | sea, weather, satellite air, place and land from `/observations`, labelled; or a note that the first poll fills this | | `readings` | `sensor_id`, `metric`, `hours=24` (up to 168) | meant to return hourly means oldest first; see the gap below | | `history` | `sensor_id`, `metric` | every `{ts, value}` oldest first, for slow series such as `place-point / sat_buildings_yearly` | | `series` | `metric="pm25"`, `hours=24` (up to 168) | aligned hourly arrays: indoor, outdoor, model | | `alerts` | `limit=10` (up to 100), `since_hours=0` | the most recent alerts: `id`, `ts`, `rule_id`, `sensor_id`, `level`, `text` and `acted_at`. With `since_hours`, `{since_hours, count, alerts}`: `count` is every alert in the window, `alerts` the newest `limit` with their text cut to 160 characters | | `report_latest` | none | the last report row | | `report_bundle` | `hours=6` (1 to 168) | every number the report was written from | | `cells` | none | the Fab City Index cells with value, unit and state | | `packs` | none | the loaded packs: id, kind, description | | `export_day` | `day?` (default yesterday) | the open-data export for that day | | `learned` | `query?`, `scale?` | with nothing, what the house learned: what worked, what is usual, the alerts that may not fit, each in the node's own sentence. With `query` (a few keywords) it searches those and the diary of days, weeks, months and years; `scale` narrows to one size, and alone gives the newest. Answers only while `AGENT_PREFER=private` and no model sits at an address outside your network, and says why otherwise | | `settings_get` | none | every runtime setting with its group, help and value; the node's secrets and the keys a pack lists under `secrets:` are masked, bootstrap keys are read-only | | `maintenance` | `task`: update, backup, restore, restart, logs, doctor, storage, ui, telegram | the `planetai` command to run on the node, what it does and where. It runs nothing | | `act` | `alert_id`, `note` (required), `agent="agent"` | writes: records `stage: acted` for that alert with the agent as actor, and returns `{recorded, alert_id, by}` | | `report_now` | `agent="agent"` | writes: a report, written and sent now | | `settings_set` | `changes: {KEY: value}`, `agent="agent"` | writes: changes runtime settings, live within 20 seconds; a blank returns the key to `.env` | | `run_pack_script` | `pack`, `script`, `args?`, `agent="agent"` | runs code: `packs/<pack>/<script>.py` inside the container (15-minute limit), and returns exit code, stdout, stderr and `by`. Every script of a core pack runs. A wild pack's script runs only if its `pack.yaml` lists it under `agent_scripts:`, otherwise the answer is an `error` pointing to `planetai run <pack> <script>` on the node's terminal. A pack's `adapter.py` is never a script here, and a pack the node does not load (left out of `PACKS_ENABLED`, or refused by its `requires:`) runs nothing | > **Gap in v0.90.0.** `readings` answers with its error for every sensor. It looks the sensor up at the top level of > `/sparks`, and the hourly means sit under `series`. Use `series` or `history` instead. `act` refuses a blank note and the placeholders that stand in for a person's words (`acted`, `acknowledged`, `done`, `ok`, `n/a`, `-`, `acted (via reticulum)`), and tells the agent to ask what the person did. On a node with `DECISION_REQUIRED=1` it gets 409 until a decision has been recorded on the dashboard against the same alert. No tool records a decision, and `act` always writes `acted`. The read routes `GET /shape`, `GET /effect` and `GET /reach` have no tool of their own.

title: MCP server and tools · The audit trail
text: The name that reaches the record is the tool's `agent` argument, and where it lands depends on the tool. `act` sends it to `POST /actions` as the row's `actor`. `settings_set` sends it as the `X-Agent` header, and `PUT /settings` writes it as the actor of an `actions` row with `stage='settings'`. `report_now` sends the header too, but `POST /report/now` records no actor, and `run_pack_script` records nothing, it only echoes the name back as `by`. No tool reads the `X-Agent` header a client sends on `/mcp` itself. The default is `agent`, so ask your client to pass its own name, `kitchen-claude` for example, in that argument. The household's bot shows up as `local-model/<rung>`, because its loop fills the argument in when the model leaves it out. Two agents on one node should read each other's rows before acting.

title: MCP server and tools · What the tools will not do
text: No tool prints `.env` or a token, and `settings_get` shows the node's own secrets as `•••• set`. A pack's key is masked only when that pack lists it under `secrets:` in its `pack.yaml`. A key it does not list there is shown in full, so a wild pack that holds a token should list it. The container has neither Docker nor git, which is why `maintenance` hands the command back instead of running it. `act` records what a person said they did and makes up nothing. The server's own instructions to a model ask for one clear sentence before a list, and never to reveal a token.

title: MCP server and tools · For a shell agent
text: `planetai status --json`, `doctor --json`, `sensors --json`, `cells --json`, and `planetai setup --answers node.json` to install without a terminal. `planetai snapshot` writes one JSON of everything the node answers, for a design round or a bug report. It asks with the admin token, so it holds more than a stranger sees (the alerts, the ledger with its notes taken out, 24 hours of aggregates), and it holds no raw readings and no token.

title: MCP server and tools · Where this leads
text: The household's own model uses a smaller set of the same tools on Telegram: [The bot](bot.md).

title: Packs that ship
text: The twenty-five core packs in `packs/`, five data and twenty code, hold everything the node knows about a place, and no rule in `app/` says what PM2.5 means for a household or where the nearest fab lab is. For each pack this page says what it reads, what it says, its rules and where each threshold comes from, its settings, and what it does not know. How a pack is built and loaded is on [Packs](packs.md). Wild packs, such as `xiaomi-air` and `posidonia`, are listed at [fabcity/planetai-wild-packs](https://github.com/fabcity/planetai-wild-packs) and added with `planetai packs add`. A pack is `code` when its folder has any `.py` file, and a code pack's adapter and hooks run only with `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE=1`; `make` also needs `MAKE_ENABLED=1` and `fire` `FIRE_ENABLED=1`. A pack that names its own `switch:` runs on that switch alone: `bali-air-dispatch` on `BAD_ENABLED`, `home-assistant` on `HA_DISCOVERY`, `smartcitizen`, `airgradient` and `purpleair` whenever their keys are set, and `air-quality` reads the CAMS model on `OPENMETEO_ENABLED`, the key that ran it in the core. A pack's `routes.py` is mounted at start and answers 404 while the pack is off. | pack | kind | domain | rules | report | cells | scripts | settings | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `air-quality` | code | air | 4 act, 2 warn; and the event engine's 3 act, 1 warn | | 3 | | `OPENMETEO_ENABLED` (declared by the core) | | `heat` | data | heat | 2 act, 1 info; and the event engine's 3 act | | 1 | | | | `bali-air-dispatch` | code | air | none | | | | `BAD_ENABLED`, `BAD_RADIUS_KM`, `BAD_MIN_SEPARATION_M`, `BAD_EXCLUDE`, `BAD_INCLUDE_INDOOR` | | `home-assistant` | code | none | none | | | | `HA_DISCOVERY` (declared by the core) | | `smartcitizen` | code | air | none | | | | `SC_USER`, `SC_DEVICES`, `SC_EXCLUDE` (declared by the core) | | `airgradient` | code | air | none | | | | `AIRGRADIENT_HOSTS`, `SENSOR_INDOOR` (declared by the core) | | `purpleair` | code | air | none | | | | `PURPLEAIR_HOSTS`, `SENSOR_INDOOR` (declared by the core) | | `nearby` | code | air | 1 act, 1 info | `alone` | | `stations` `status` `verify` `backfill` | `BAD_BACKFILL_DAYS`; the ring's are `bali-air-dispatch`'s | | `season` | code | air | 1 info | `record` | | `window` | | | `insight` | data | cross-domain | 2 info | `digest` | | | | | `cold-start` | data | cross-domain | 3 info | | | | | | `forecast` | code | weather | none | `ahead` | | `fetch` `status` `verify` `windfield` | `FORECAST_*` | | `coast` | code | coast | 2 info | | 1 | | `COAST_MAX_KM` | | `surface-heat` | code | heat | none | `ground` | | | `SURFACE_HEAT_*` | | `earth` | code | land | none | | 1 | `fetch` `change` `frames` `status` `verify` `similar` | `EARTH_*` | | `terrain` | code | water | none | | | `coverage` `fetch` `verify` | `TERRAIN_*` | | `earth-engine` | code | land | none | | 1 | `timelapse` `verify` `basemap` | `EE_*`, `GROUND_SAT_WIDE_KM` | | `place` | code | place | 1 info | | 1 | `refresh` `gaps` `verify` `basemap` | `PLACE_*`, `GROUND_*` | | `make` | code | make | none | the nearest-lab line | | | `MAKE_*` | | `fire` | code | air | 1 act, 1 warn, 1 info | | | | `FIRE_*`, `FIRMS_MAP_KEY` | | `open-data-health` | data | governance | 1 warn | | 2 | | `CKAN_PORTALS` (core adapter) | | `thingdata` | code | repair | 1 warn | | 2 | | `THINGDATA_*` | | `things` | code | things | none | | | | none (the Telegram bot's token, the core's) | | `eyes` | code | species | none | | | | `CAPTURES_DIR`, `EYES_MODEL`, `SPECIES_MATCH` (declared by the core) | | `example-cooking-hours` | data | (none) | 1 info | | | | | That is 33 rules with a message (26, and the 7 only the event engine reads), 5 report contributors and 12 cells. Every message is in `en`, `id` and `es`; the node picks `message[ALERT_LOCALE]` and falls back to `en`. Cooldowns below are in minutes, per `(rule, sensor_id)`. A report contributor (`contributes: report`) has no message and is never sent: its row goes into the report bundle under the rule's id.

title: Packs that ship · air-quality
text: PM2.5 rules built around the decision a household faces, whether the room is better or worse than the street and whether the windows should be open or shut, and three Index cells. It was written at Kuta Selatan, Bali, against a Smart Citizen kit and the public stations from Bali Air Dispatch. | | | |---|---| | Kind | code | | Domain | `air` | | Requires node | `>=0.83.0` | | Metrics | `pm25`, `pm10`, `pm1`, `humidity`; from CAMS `pm25_model`, `pm10_model`, `dust`, `aod`, `co`, `no2`, `o3`, `uv_index` | | Scales | community, city | | Needs | a low-cost PM sensor at the address, and for the comparison rules at least one outdoor reference (below) | | Scripts | none | | Settings | `OPENMETEO_ENABLED` runs its adapter, the CAMS model at the node's point each poll; the SQL reads `planetai.lat` and `planetai.lon` and whatever sources the node polls | ### Rules Thresholds are US EPA and WHO 2021 (`thresholds:` in `pack.yaml`): 35.5 µg/m³ is unhealthy for sensitive groups, 55.5 µg/m³ unhealthy, and 15 µg/m³ the WHO 24-hour guideline. The comparison rules take the ambient reference in a fixed order: the node's own outdoor sensors first, then the three nearest public outdoor sensors (`NOT local`, `kind='sensor'`, silent under 120 minutes), then the CAMS model (`observations` where `sensor_id='cams-point'` and `metric='pm25_model'`). | rule | level | cooldown | fires when | |---|---|---|---| | `indoor_pm25_high` | act | 120 | a local indoor sensor's 15-minute PM2.5 mean is over 35.5 | | `outside_worse_keep_shut` | act | 180 | the best ambient reference is over 35.5 and more than 1.5 times the indoor 1-hour mean | | `inside_worse_ventilate` | act | 180 | the indoor 1-hour mean is over 15 and more than 1.5 times the best ambient reference | | `outdoor_pm25_high` | act | 180 | a local outdoor sensor's 1-hour mean is over 55.5 | | `indoor_spike` | warn | 90 | an indoor 15-minute mean is at least 12 and at least 2.5 times the greater of its 24-hour mean and 2 | | `outdoor_spike` | warn | 90 | an outdoor sensor (local, or within about 0.03° of the node) silent under 60 minutes has a 15-minute mean of at least 15 and at least 2.5 times the greater of its 24-hour mean and 2 | `indoor_pm25_high` and `outdoor_pm25_high` declare `watch:` on `pm25` at their own line, so `GET /effect` can say how long after an act the hourly mean came back under it. The other four have no single line to watch. Four more rules carry a `kind:` and only the event engine reads them ([Alerts](alerts.md#the-event-engine)): skipped under `ALERT_ENGINE=rules`, and under `shadow` and `events` folded into one `air` event, each returning `value`, `line`, `over` and `where` (`inside` or `outside`). Cooldown 60 each. The numbers are starting values from a replay of node #1's first month. | rule | kind | level | `over` when | |---|---|---|---| | `air_spike` | spike | warn | a local sensor's latest 15-minute mean is at least 12 above the mean of the preceding hour and at least 10 above this room's 90th percentile for the local hour (a rise of 7 keeps an open event open) | | `air_unusual` | unusual | act | every 15-minute mean of the last hour is at least 15 above this room's usual 90th percentile for the hour (an hourly mean 10 above keeps an open event open) | | `air_sustained` | sustained | act | the 15-minute means over the last hour are all at least 35 µg/m³ (a mean of 30 keeps it open) | | `air_extreme` | danger | act | the latest 15-minute mean is at least 125.5 µg/m³ (115 keeps it open) | ### Cells | cell | unit | state | min_buckets | what the SQL counts | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Environmental\|Community` | µg/m³ PM2.5 (24h mean, sensors in this node's custody) | live | 12 | mean of `readings_1h.mean` over 24 hours for sensors where `sensors.custody` | | `Environmental\|Community` | % of days over the WHO 24h PM2.5 guideline (30d, local outdoor) | partial | 20 | of the days with at least 12 hourly buckets from custody outdoor sensors, the share whose day mean is over 15 | | `Environmental\|City` | µg/m³ PM2.5 (24h mean, public reference stations) | partial | | 24-hour mean over sensors that are `NOT local AND NOT indoor AND kind='sensor'` | The core demotes the first cell to `partial` until it has 12 hourly buckets and enough in-custody sensors. The third is never `live`, because those stations are not the node's measurement. ### What it does not know The thresholds and the wording are Bali's. For another place, copy the folder, change both, publish it as `planetai-pack-air-<yourplace>` and list it at [fabcity/planetai-wild-packs](https://github.com/fabcity/planetai-wild-packs).

title: Packs that ship · heat
text: Turns the temperature and humidity the node already stores into three sentences about heat and one Index cell. Apparent temperature is Steadman's no-wind form as published by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology, `AT = T + 0.33·e − 4.0`, with `e` the vapour pressure in hPa. It was written for a humid tropical house in Kuta Selatan, 8°S at sea level, where it is about 26 to 31 °C and 50 to 75% RH all year, and every threshold is that place's. | | | |---|---| | Kind | data | | Domain | `heat` | | Requires node | `>=0.10.0` | | Metrics | `temp`, `humidity` | | Scales | community | | Needs | a local indoor sensor reporting both `temp` and `humidity` (Smart Citizen, AirGradient and a BME680 on a Tracker all do) | | Scripts | none | | Settings | none | ### Rules | rule | level | cooldown | fires when | |---|---|---|---| | `heat_stress_now` | act | 1440 | a local indoor sensor's 15-minute temperature and humidity give an apparent temperature of 35 °C or more | | `heat_danger` | act | 120 | the same, at 40 °C or more | | `night_no_relief` | info | 1440 | over the last 12 hours, in the local hours outside 07 to 21, a local indoor sensor's hourly minimum never fell to 28 °C, with at least 5 buckets | 40 °C is the heat-index "danger" line, and 28 °C overnight is the WHO ceiling for restorative sleep. 35 °C is the pack's own, measured at node #1: the usual "extreme caution" line of 32 °C is the year-round baseline in Kuta Selatan and fired twenty times in two days, while 35 °C is the hot room's 90th percentile. The cooldown keeps it to once a room a day. Both act rules declare `watch:` on `apparent` at their own line. Three more rules carry a `kind:` and fold into one `heat` event, as in `air-quality`. They read `recent_15m`'s `apparent` and `usual_by_hour` for indoor sensors only, and leave out a sensor whose `temp` channel is not declared ambient, such as a Meshtastic radio's own box. Cooldown 60 each. | rule | kind | level | `over` when | |---|---|---|---| | `heat_unusual` | unusual | act | every 15-minute mean apparent temperature of the last hour is at least 2 °C above this room's usual 90th percentile for the hour (an hourly mean 1 °C above keeps an open event open) | | `heat_sustained` | sustained | act | the room has been at 35 °C or more for at least 3 hours, and for more than its usual number of such hours (a latest mean of 34 keeps an open event open) | | `heat_extreme` | danger | act | the latest 15-minute mean is at least 40 °C (39 keeps it open) | ### Cells | cell | unit | state | min_buckets | what the SQL counts | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Social\|Community` | hours in 30d with indoor apparent temperature ≥ 32 °C | live | 12 | custody indoor hourly buckets with AT at or above 32, divided by the number of distinct sensors | The cell keeps 32 °C where the rule moved to 35: 32 is right for counting exposure, which is what a cell does, and wrong for interrupting a household, which is what a rule does. ### What it does not know Every rule and the cell read local indoor sensors only, because the no-wind Steadman form is the indoor form; a node whose only local sensors are outdoors gets no heat alerts. The pack knows nothing of radiant heat or airflow, and its calibration rests on five dry-season days at one house, with a highest AT of 36.5 °C. To move the line, change the `>= 35` in `heat_stress_now` to near the 90th percentile of your hottest indoor sensor.

title: Packs that ship · bali-air-dispatch
text: Reads the island's public air stations around the node from Bali Air Dispatch, one key-free archive of eight networks (Nafas, IQAir, PurpleAir, AQICN, OpenAQ, AirGradient, Smart Citizen, Airly). It stores them as other people's stations (`local=false`, at any distance), so the node can tell the lane from the island. It says nothing itself: `nearby` and `season` read what it stores. Bali only. | | | |---|---| | Kind | code, run by its own switch (`switch: BAD_ENABLED`) | | Domain | `air` | | Requires node | `>=0.82.3` | | Metrics | `pm25`, `pm25_raw`, `pm10`, `pm1`, `temp`, `humidity`, `aqi` | | Scales | community | | Sources | `environmental/community/bali-air-dispatch` | | Needs | network to `baliairdispatch.com`; `NODE_LAT` and `NODE_LON` | | Rules and cells | none: peers never drive an alert (`thresholds:` in `pack.yaml` says so) | | Attribution | Bali Air Dispatch, baliairdispatch.com, and the network named in each row's `source` | The sensor ids are `bad-<station>` and the source is `baliairdispatch`. Its channels are in its own `channels.yml`. It declares `stations:` in `pack.yaml` (`source`, `prefix`, `radius`, `box`, `url`, `attribution`), which is how the "Air stations nearby" source, `GET /nearby` and the ring on the map find it without naming it. A node inside the `box`, south Bali to north Bali, with the pack off is told to turn it on; a node anywhere else is told nothing. On `planetai update`, a node that lists its packs in `PACKS_ENABLED` and has `BAD_ENABLED=1` gets `bali-air-dispatch` added to the list. ### Settings | setting | default | meaning | |---|---|---| | `BAD_ENABLED` | `0`; the bali preset `1` | the pack's switch. It runs the adapter without `PACKS_ALLOW_CODE` | | `BAD_RADIUS_KM` | `15`; the bali preset `8` | ring radius in km. 15 is the tightest that leaves `nearby` its two-station floor at node #1 with room to spare | | `BAD_MIN_SEPARATION_M` | `150` | a station closer to the node than this is excluded as the node's own kit | | `BAD_EXCLUDE` | empty | station ids excluded by hand | | `BAD_INCLUDE_INDOOR` | `0` | `1` keeps stations the archive marks `suspected_indoor` | It also reads `SC_USER`, `SC_DEVICES`, `SC_EXCLUDE` and `AIRGRADIENT_HOSTS`, to know which devices this node already polls. ### What it does not know It keeps the node's own kit out of the ring by four tests: identity (a device this node polls, at any distance), proximity (within `BAD_MIN_SEPARATION_M`), by hand (`BAD_EXCLUDE`), and one device on two networks (an AirGradient unit mirrored by OpenAQ, collapsed on the same name within the separation radius). It cannot know about a kit of yours it does not poll and that sits further away than the separation radius. One function, `verdicts()`, decides, and `nearby`'s scripts and `GET /nearby?audit=1` call the same one.

title: Packs that ship · smartcitizen
text: Reads this node's own Smart Citizen kits from api.smartcitizen.me: the ones listed by id (`SC_DEVICES`), and the ones in the household's account (`SC_USER`) that published in the last three days, less `SC_EXCLUDE`. Every one is the house's own, so every one is stored `local`, indoor or outdoor from the kit's own `exposure`. And the kits and DIY nodes that publish straight to this node's broker (`device/sck/#`, set up with `planetai broker`), stored as `sck-<hash>` with source `smartcitizen-direct`, and passed on to smartcitizen.me for the tokens in `SC_FORWARD`. | | | |---|---| | Kind | code, on whenever a kit is configured or a broker is set (`switch: [SC_USER, SC_DEVICES, MQTT_HOST]`) | | Domain | `air` | | Requires node | `>=0.83.0` | | Sources | `environmental/community/smart-citizen` | | Needs | network to `api.smartcitizen.me`, and to `mqtt.smartcitizen.me:8883` for the tokens in `SC_FORWARD` | | Rules and cells | none: `air-quality` and `heat` decide what the readings mean | The sensor ids are `sc-<kit>` and the source is `smartcitizen`, as they were in the core until 22 October 2026, and the direct path keeps its `sck-` ids and its `direct` key in `/health`, so a node's history carries on. Its three settings stay under Set up → Sources, where a household sets up its kits, and `SC_FORWARD` under Sharing, because it changes what leaves the house. Which kits in an account are the node's own stays in the core (`sources.smartcitizen_account`), because `bali-air-dispatch` and `nearby` ask it too. The direct path is `hooks.py`: the node subscribes to its `MQTT_TOPICS` and hands it every message on them. On `planetai update`, a node that lists its packs in `PACKS_ENABLED` and has `SC_USER`, `SC_DEVICES` or `MQTT_HOST` set gets `smartcitizen` added to the list, so it keeps reading its kits.

title: Packs that ship · airgradient
